articles.title: Contraindication-adjusted prescription omission patterns of RASi, beta-blockers, and MRAs in hospitalized heart failure: associations with 30-day and 1-year mortality.
articles.abstract: Guideline directed therapy is still underused in heart failure and little is known about how missing specific medications near discharge relates to survival. The aim of this study is to examine whether study-defined omission patterns of RASi (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or ARNIs), beta-blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) in the final 48 h before discharge were associated with short-term and 1-year mortality among hospitalized adults with heart failure. Adult admissions with a recorded heart failure diagnosis were identified using ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes. The three classes were RASi, beta-blockers, and MRAs (SGLT2 inhibitors were not included). A contraindication-adjusted operational framework was used to identify admissions without selected laboratory or hemodynamic barriers to these therapies and to classify late-hospital prescription omission patterns. Final-48-h orders were a proxy for treatment near discharge, not a reconciled discharge list. This framework did not establish heart failure phenotype-specific guideline eligibility. Associations with mortality within 30 and 365 days after discharge were evaluated using multivariable regression models. The final analytic cohort included 57,098 admissions from 24,922 patients. The reference group with prescriptions for all three study classes was small whereas omission of 2 or 3 therapies was substantially more common across the cohort. Admissions with prescriptions for all three study classes had the lowest 365-day mortality (13.88%). Crude 365-day mortality was higher in all omission groups, reaching 30.84% when RASi and beta-blocker were omitted and 27.50% when all three classes were omitted. In adjusted analyses, omission of all 3 therapies was associated with higher 30-day mortality (OR = 1.67). For 365-day mortality, the strongest adverse association was observed for omission of renin-angiotensin system inhibitor plus beta-blocker (HR = 1.33). Late-hospital omission patterns involving RASi and omission of all three study therapies were associated with higher post-discharge mortality. As heart failure phenotype and left-ventricular ejection fraction were not incorporated into the eligibility definition, these findings should be interpreted as prognostic associations of prescribing patterns rather than causal effects of withholding guideline-indicated HFrEF therapy.

articles.title: Combined melatonin and edaravone therapy attenuates methylmercury-induced amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-like neurodegeneration through GLP-1 modulation and myelin preservation.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive and fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the selective degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons, resulting in progressive muscle weakness, paralysis, and respiratory failure. Despite the availability of disease-modifying therapies, current treatment options provide only modest clinical benefits, highlighting the need for novel therapeutic strategies targeting multiple pathological mechanisms. Melatonin, a pleiotropic neuroprotective molecule with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-apoptotic properties, has emerged as a promising candidate; however, its influence on glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)-associated neuroprotective signaling and related molecular events in ALS remains poorly understood. Therefore, the present study investigated the neuroprotective efficacy of melatonin in a methylmercury (MTMR)-induced rat model of ALS and explored its effects on GLP-1-associated molecular alterations, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, apoptosis, neurotransmitter homeostasis, demyelination, and neuronal injury. Molecular docking analysis was performed to predict the interaction of melatonin with proteins implicated in ALS pathology. Adult Wistar rats were exposed to MTMR (5 mg/kg, p.o.) for 21 days to induce ALS-like neurodegeneration, followed by treatment with melatonin (5 or 10 mg/kg, i.p.), edaravone (3 mg/kg, i.p.), or their combination for an additional 21 days. Neurobehavioral performance, biochemical alterations, hematological parameters, molecular biomarkers, and histopathological changes were subsequently evaluated. MTMR administration produced profound motor deficits accompanied by reduced GLP-1 levels, neurotransmitter imbalance, increased neuroinflammatory and apoptotic markers, elevated neurofilament light chain (NEFL), skeletal muscle injury, methylmercury accumulation, and extensive myelin and neuronal damage. Melatonin treatment significantly attenuated these pathological alterations in a dose-dependent manner by increasing GLP-1 levels, improving antioxidant status, reducing inflammatory and apoptotic responses, restoring neurotransmitter balance, preserving myelin integrity, and improving neuronal morphology across multiple brain regions and the spinal cord. Molecular docking further predicted favorable interactions between melatonin and several proteins associated with ALS pathophysiology, supporting its potential as a multitarget therapeutic agent. In most outcome measures, combined treatment with melatonin and edaravone produced greater neuroprotective effects than either intervention alone. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that melatonin substantially attenuates methylmercury-induced ALS-like neuropathology through coordinated modulation of multiple pathological processes associated with neurodegeneration. Although the precise molecular mechanisms require further experimental validation, the observed restoration of GLP-1 levels together with improvements in oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, apoptosis, neurotransmitter homeostasis, and myelin integrity suggests that melatonin may represent a promising adjunctive therapeutic strategy for ALS.

articles.title: Temocillin versus piperacillin-tazobactam for ICU pneumonia caused by Enterobacterales: a Belgian single-centre retrospective study.
articles.journal: European journal of clinical microbiology & infectious diseases : official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: The aim of this study was to explore the clinical outcomes of ICU patients with Enterobacterales pneumonia treated with temocillin or piperacillin-tazobactam.

METHODS: This retrospective, single-centre study included ICU patients with culture-confirmed Enterobacterales pneumonia over 5 years. Only isolates susceptible to both study antibiotics were included. Patients were excluded if they received the study antibiotic for less than 48 h, had more than 72 h of prior empirical therapy, or required escalation to broad-spectrum antibiotics for a new infection. Primary outcomes were 28-day mortality and clinical failure, and secondary outcomes included ICU and hospital length of stay. Multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to assess the association between treatment group and the primary outcomes.

RESULTS: 167 ICU patients (66 temocillin, 101 piperacillin-tazobactam) were included. Baseline characteristics, comorbidities, and severity markers were largely comparable, although in the temocillin group pneumonia more often developed later during ICU stay and treatment was less frequently initiated empirically. 28-day mortality occurred in 23% and 29% of patients in the temocillin and piperacillin-tazobactam groups, respectively (p = 0.39), while clinical failure occurred in 47% and 46%, respectively (p = 0.86). In multivariable analysis, the adjusted OR for temocillin versus piperacillin-tazobactam was 0.931 (95% CI, 0.380-2.276; p = 0.87) for 28-day mortality and 1.224 (95% CI, 0.591-2.536; p = 0.59) for clinical failure.

CONCLUSION: Although the study was not designed to establish non-inferiority of temocillin and the sample size was limited, our findings raise the possibility that temocillin may be a viable treatment option for Enterobacterales-associated pneumonia. Prospective studies are needed to clarify its role.

articles.title: Clinical Trajectories and Cardiac Phenotypes in Danon Disease.
articles.abstract: Danon disease is a rare X-linked lysosomal cardioskeletal myopathy caused by loss-of-function variants in LAMP2, which impair autophagosome-lysosome fusion and lead to accumulation of autophagic vacuoles in cardiomyocytes. Although cardiac penetrance is high in both sexes, the natural history differs markedly by sex. Males typically present in childhood or adolescence with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy, and intellectual disability, and often progress to heart failure or ventricular arrhythmias by early adulthood. Females typically present later in life with a cardiac-predominant phenotype that more often evolves to dilated cardiomyopathy, although a subset develops an early onset, severe phenotype reminiscent of male hemizygotes. Pooled case data suggest that cumulative rates of death, heart transplantation, or ventricular assist device implantation are similar between sexes but occur approximately 2 decades later in females, indicating that women may be delayed rather than spared. Ventricular preexcitation, mediated by fasciculoventricular or extranodal accessory pathways, and a characteristic cardiac magnetic resonance pattern of late gadolinium enhancement with mid-basal septal sparing can support the diagnosis, although septal sparing is less frequent in females. Heart transplantation remains the established treatment, and a phase 1 trial of AAV9-LAMP2B gene therapy has provided early proof-of-concept in males.

articles.title: Breaking the Barrier: MBI-LCBI and Recent Beta-lactam Exposure as Predictors of Piperacillin-Tazobactam Resistance in Pediatric Hemato-oncology Patients.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Gram-negative bloodstream infections (BSIs) in pediatric hemato-oncology patients, particularly those with neutropenia, are associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. While piperacillin-tazobactam (PTZ) remains a standard empiric therapy, increasing resistance poses a significant clinical challenge. Identifying risk factors for PTZ-resistant (PTZ-R) BSI is crucial for optimizing empiric antibiotic selection and improving clinical outcomes.

METHODS: This retrospective study (2015-2024) analyzed pediatric hemato-oncology Gram-negative BSIs at a northern Israeli tertiary center. Using clinical and microbiologic data, we performed univariate and multivariate logistic regression to identify independent predictors of PTZ resistance.

RESULTS: Overall, 284 episodes in 162 patients were evaluated for PTZ susceptibility. Seventy (24.6%) episodes in 56 (34.6%) patients were PTZ-R. Mucosal barrier injury laboratory-confirmed BSI (MBI-LCBI) accounted for 46.1% of episodes, central line-associated bloodstream infection for 50% and secondary BSI for 3.9%. MBI-LCBI (68.6% vs. 38.8%, P < 0.001), beta-lactam use within the preceding 30 days (67.2% vs. 43.2%, P < 0.001), and colonization with extended-spectrum beta-lactamases and carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (14.3% vs. 5.6%, P = 0.018) were markedly more common among PTZ-R episodes. Additionally, nonlocal residency (5.7% vs. 16.1%, P = 0.014) and hematologic malignancy (85.5% vs. 62.5%, P = 0.003) were significantly more prevalent in patients with PTZ-R episodes. In multivariate analysis, MBI-LCBI (odds ratio 3.1, 95% confidence interval 1.7-6) and recent beta-lactam exposure (odds ratio 2.2, 95% confidence interval 1.2-4.1) were independent predictors of PTZ-R. Thirty-day mortality occurred in 9 (4.2%) cases; all were PTZ sensitive (P = 0.119).

CONCLUSIONS: High PTZ-R in pediatric hemato-oncology BSIs is driven by recent beta-lactam use and MBI-LCBI. Identifying these risk factors may support the selection of appropriate empiric therapy for high-risk patients.

articles.title: Extended Versus Short Dual Antiplatelet Therapy Duration After Percutaneous Coronary Intervention for Chronic Total Occlusion: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: Chronic total occlusion (CTO) percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is associated with substantial ischemic risk, yet the optimal duration of dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) after successful CTO-PCI remains uncertain. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing extended DAPT (>12 months) with short-term DAPT (≤12 months) following CTO-PCI. Four electronic biomedical databases were searched from inception to September 2026. Comparative studies evaluating adult patients undergoing successful CTO-PCI with drug-eluting stent implantation were eligible. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using a random-effects model. Three retrospective cohort studies including 3362 patients were identified, with 1761 receiving extended DAPT and 1601 receiving short-term DAPT. Extended DAPT was associated with a significantly lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular events compared with short-term DAPT (RR 0.68; 95% CI 0.55-0.84; P = 0.0004). There was no significant difference in all-cause death (RR 0.25; 95% CI 0.04-1.41; P = 0.116), myocardial infarction, stroke, cardiovascular death, major bleeding, or revascularization outcomes. However, extended DAPT was associated with a significantly higher risk of total bleeding (RR 2.34; 95% CI 1.31-4.20; P = 0.0043). Among patients undergoing successful CTO-PCI, extended DAPT was associated with lower major adverse cardiovascular events but increased total bleeding compared with DAPT ≤12 months.

articles.title: Overlapping roles of dysregulated glycolysis in the pathophysiology of diabetes and cancer.
articles.abstract: Emerging evidence highlights a strong association between type 2 diabetes (T2D) and increased cancer risk, with partially overlapping metabolic disruptions potentially driving both diseases. Chronic hyperglycemia, a hallmark of T2D, disrupts glycolytic flux and contributes to the accumulation of toxic intermediates, driving cellular damage and diabetic complications. Specifically, dysregulation of glycolytic enzymes diverts metabolites into harmful pathways, promoting oxidative and glycative stress across multiple cell types. Similar metabolic disturbances support cancer development and progression by fueling rapid tumor cell proliferation. This review explores the role of abnormal glycolysis as a potential mechanistic link between T2D and cancer, detailing shared enzymatic alterations and metabolic pathway shifts. Additionally, it discusses pharmacological therapeutic strategies targeting glycolysis-related abnormalities common to both diseases, emphasizing the need for balanced metabolic modulation.

articles.title: Does a Within-patient Rise in Infliximab Area Under the Curve Predict Subsequent Infection?
Home-based nurse-led self-management support for heart failure: a randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract:
AIM: To evaluate the effect of a nurse-led, stage-tailored home-based self-management and follow-up programme on self-care behaviour in people with heart failure.

BACKGROUND: People with heart failure require ongoing education, symptom monitoring, and self-management support after specialist assessment. However, access to structured centre-based cardiac rehabilitation may be limited. A nurse-led home-based model may help bridge the gap between specialist cardiology care and community-based long-term support, particularly where rehabilitation services are unavailable.

METHODS: In this parallel-group randomized controlled trial, adults aged 40-75 years with New York Heart Association class I-III heart failure and ejection fraction >30% were allocated to a 12-week home-based programme or usual care. The intervention was delivered through nurse-led home visits and telephone follow-up for clinically stable patients who could not access structured centre-based rehabilitation. The intervention group received home visits and telephone follow-up (n = 32), while the control group received usual care (n = 31). The primary outcome was self-care behaviour. Secondary outcomes were quality of life, self-efficacy, and physical capacity. Exploratory clinical outcomes were body composition, ejection fraction, and HbA1c level.

FINDINGS: At 12 weeks, the intervention group had better self-care scores than the control group (17.78 ± 2.93 vs 40.00 ± 6.49). Secondary outcomes also favoured the intervention group, with better quality of life scores, higher self-efficacy scores, and greater 6-minute walk distance. Exploratory clinical outcomes showed changes in some parameters, including ejection fraction and body-fluid values. Most intervention participants reached the Transtheoretical Model action stage, and New York Heart Association class improved significantly. This primary health care-relevant home-based model was associated with improved self-care behaviour and may support continuity of care for people with heart failure after specialist cardiology assessment when centre-based rehabilitation is unavailable.

CONCLUSION: The programme improved self-care in people with heart failure and showed potential to support home-based self-management when centre-based cardiac rehabilitation was unavailable.

articles.title: Cardiac hemorrhage precedes hypertension-induced fibrosis in plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 deficient mice.
articles.abstract:
AIMS: Plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) regulates plasmin-mediated proteolysis, thereby influencing vascular stability and tissue remodeling. Angiotensin II (AngII) induces an increase in PAI-1 during the development of ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm (ATAA). The initial purpose of this study was to determine whether deletion of PAI-1 influenced development of ATAA. Subsequently, this study aimed to define the early pathological events preceding cardiac fibrosis in PAI-1 deficiency and the structural domain responsible for its protective effect.

METHODS AND RESULTS: AngII was infused for 4 weeks in whole-body PAI-1 deficient (PAI-1-/-) mice and their wild-type littermates (PAI-1+/+) to examine the role of PAI-1 in ATAA. PAI-1 deficiency did not alter AngII-induced aortopathy but revealed a striking cardiac phenotype characterized by replacement fibrosis predominantly within the epicardium and posterior septum. Ferric iron, indicative of prior hemorrhage, was coincident with fibrosis. Similar phenotypes were observed in PAI-1-/- mice infused with norepinephrine for 4 weeks. To define the pathological events preceding cardiac fibrosis, either AngII or norepinephrine was infused for 1 week in PAI-1+/+ or -/- mice. Both infusions induced extensive epicardial hemorrhage and posterior septal fibrosis in PAI-1-/- mice. To explore the initiation of cardiac pathology, AngII was infused for approximately 1 day. PAI-1-/- mice developed diffuse hemorrhage and cardiomyocyte injury localized to the posterior septum, pathologic changes that preceded overt fibrosis. Finally, to determine the protective domain of PAI-1, saline or AngII was administered to mice harboring loss-of-function point mutations in the protease inhibitory (PAI-1Ala/Ala) or somatomedin B-binding domains (PAI-1AK/AK). Compared to saline infusion, 1 week of AngII induced hemorrhage and heterogeneous fibrosis in PAI-1Ala/Ala, but not PAI-1AK/AK mice.

CONCLUSIONS: These findings support that, under hemodynamic stress, PAI-1 deficiency promotes early cardiac hemorrhage and cardiomyocyte injury that lead to fibrosis. Mutational studies implicate dysregulated plasmin generation as an initiator of cardiac injury and fibrosis.

articles.title: Cortisol in cardio-kidney-metabolic disease.
articles.abstract: Despite guideline-directed therapy, many patients with cardio-kidney-metabolic (CKM) disease remain uncontrolled due to therapeutic inertia, adherence barriers, and underrecognized secondary causes. Hypercortisolism, ranging from mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS) to overt Cushing syndrome, is an increasingly recognized contributor. MACS is associated with a 2.5-fold higher risk of cardiovascular death and increased prevalence of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), and kidney impairment. Cortisol excess promotes muscle insulin resistance, hepatic gluconeogenesis, β-cell dysfunction, sodium retention, and vascular remodelling, worsening glycaemia and blood pressure, leading to poor CKM outcomes. Recent prospective studies suggest that hypercortisolism is more prevalent than previously suspected in selected CKM phenotypes, including 24% in patients with difficult-to-control T2DM in CATALYST and 27% in patients with resistant hypertension in MOMENTUM. The overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test remains the diagnostic test of choice. Therapeutic strategies include adrenal steroidogenesis inhibitors, glucocorticoid receptor antagonists, and pituitary-directed therapies in selected cases, while surgery remains the first-line treatment for surgically remediable disease. This review summarizes the epidemiology and mechanisms linking cortisol excess to CKM dysfunction, and also highlights the need for clinical trials, standardized diagnostic thresholds, and assays to enable integration of cortisol-targeted therapies into management pathways to mitigate residual CKM risk. This review will serve as a practical guide for cardiologists to manage a potentially reversible contributor to poor CKM control.

articles.title: Ergonomic interventions for treating work-related complaints of the arm, neck or shoulder in adults.
articles.journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
articles.abstract:
RATIONALE: Work-related complaints of the arm, neck or shoulder (CANS) are disorders that develop as a result of repetitive movements, awkward postures or external forces (e.g. vibrating tools), and significantly affect the working population globally. Ergonomic interventions (which aim to enhance efficiency and comfort in the working environment) can be used to manage CANS. This review is based on a new protocol but updates part of a 2013 Cochrane review.

OBJECTIVES: To assess the effectiveness of ergonomic interventions for work-related complaints of the arm, neck or shoulder (CANS) in adults, in terms of their effects on pain, functional status and work-related outcomes.

SEARCH METHODS: We updated the 2013 review searches, searching from 31 May 2013 to 1 June 2026 in eight bibliographic databases and one trials register.

ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs), cluster-RCTs and quasi-RCTs that evaluated single or combined ergonomic interventions (e.g. office furniture, biomechanical or ergonomic education) compared to no treatment/usual care/placebo or another active intervention (exercise/another ergonomic intervention/other treatment), or as an add-on treatment.

OUTCOMES: Critical outcomes: pain, functional status (disability) and work-related outcomes (e.g. sickness absence, return to work, productivity loss at work, change of occupation). Important outcomes: global perceived effect (e.g. overall improvement), quality of life, healthcare consumption, and recurrence of injury, disorder or complaint. We prioritised outcomes in the short term (up to three months after the intervention) and were also interested in long-term results (over three months).

RISK OF BIAS: We assessed the risk of bias in the studies using Cochrane's RoB 1 tool.

SYNTHESIS METHODS: Two authors independently screened the search records, selected trials, extracted data and assessed risk of bias. When we judged studies to have sufficient clinical and statistical homogeneity, we performed meta-analysis. We assessed overall certainty of the evidence using GRADE for key outcomes at the short-term time point.

INCLUDED STUDIES: We brought forward 13 studies from the 2013 review. We identified two new articles relating to one of those 13 studies, along with seven new studies. Therefore, in total, we included 20 studies involving 2478 participants. In 16 studies, the participants had non-specific CANS; in four studies, the participants had specific CANS (e.g. carpal tunnel syndrome).

SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: Results below are presented at the short-term time point. Ergonomic interventions versus no treatment, usual care or placebo in people with CANS Data were available only for trials that focused on non-specific CANS. Ergonomic interventions may result in little to no difference in pain compared to no treatment, usual care or placebo in people with CANS (SMD -0.23, 95% CI -0.54 to 0.08; 4 RCTs, 692 participants; low-certainty evidence). Ergonomic interventions probably result in little to no difference in functional status (disability) compared to being on a waiting list (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.34; 1 RCT (2 comparisons), 383 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Ergonomic interventions may result in little to no difference in sick leave compared to no treatment (MD for continuous data -0.32, 95% CI -0.73 to 0.09; 1 RCT, 98 participants; low-certainty evidence; RR for dichotomous data 0.87, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.21; 3 RCTs, 759 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Ergonomic interventions probably result in little to no difference in recovery compared to no treatment (RR 1.32, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.97; 1 RCT (2 comparisons), 386 participants, moderate-certainty evidence). Ergonomic interventions may result in little to no difference in quality of life compared to no treatment (MD 0.10, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.20; 1 RCT, 68 participants; low-certainty evidence). Ergonomic interventions may result in little to no difference in healthcare consumption compared to no treatment when measured using continuous outcomes (MD -0.10. 95% CI -0.30 to 0.10; 1 RCT, 68 participants; low-certainty evidence), and may result in a reduction in healthcare consumption compared to usual care when measured using dichotomous outcomes (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.78; 1 RCT, 210 participants; low-certainty evidence). No data were available for recurrence of injury, disorder or complaint. Ergonomic intervention versus active intervention (exercise or another type of ergonomic intervention or other treatment) in people with CANS Data were available from trials involving participants with specific CANS and with non-specific CANS. The evidence is very uncertain about the effects of ergonomic interventions on pain (SMD 0.41, 95% CI -0.02 to 0.84; 8 RCTs, 364 participants; very-low-certainty evidence) and on functional status (disability) (SMD -0.09, 95% CI -0.85 to 0.68; 3 RCTs, 180 participants; very-low-certainty evidence) compared to active intervention in people with specific or non-specific CANS. Intense ergonomic interventions may result in little to no difference in recovery (RR 1.29, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.94; 1 RCT, 257 participants; low-certainty evidence) or healthcare consumption (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.47; 1 RCT, 217 participants; low-certainty evidence) compared to ergonomic education in people with non-specific CANS. Ergonomic interventions may improve quality of life compared to exercise in people with non-specific CANS (MD -10.10, 95% CI -19.87 to -0.33; 1 RCT, 61 participants; low-certainty evidence). No data were available for work-related outcomes or recurrence of injury, disorder or complaint. Ergonomic intervention plus another treatment versus the other treatment alone in people with CANS Data were available only from trials of participants with non-specific CANS. The evidence is very uncertain about the effects of ergonomic intervention as an add-on treatment to exercise on pain (SMD -0.50, 95% CI -1.64 to 0.63; 2 RCTs, 137 participants; very-low-certainty evidence). No data were available for our other outcomes of interest.

AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: Overall, ergonomic interventions for work-related CANS may have no meaningful effects on pain, function, recovery, quality of life or work-related outcomes (sick leave) compared with no treatment or usual care. Findings are inconsistent for healthcare consumption. There may be a possible benefit for quality of life when ergonomic interventions are compared to exercise. The evidence for ergonomic interventions as an add-on treatment is very uncertain. High-quality, well-designed trials are needed to establish the role of ergonomic interventions in the management of CANS.

articles.title: The Prague 2025 consensus checklist for reporting indirect outcome studies of Model 1b analytical performance specifications.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Analytical performance specifications (APS) based on the Milan Model 1b criteria investigate the impact of analytical performance of a test on clinical classification or decisions, as indirect intermediates to health outcomes of patients. In the lack of guidance for how Model 1b APS should be developed, the objective was to provide generic methodological standards for the design, conduct and reporting of indirect outcome studies for Model 1b APS.

METHODS: An interactive workshop followed by several online meetings of experts was organised to discuss the key challenges and limitations of and to develop a checklist of essential reporting elements for Model 1b APS studies.

RESULTS: The checklist for reporting Model 1b APS includes 17 essential items with explanatory notes and cross-references to 25 items of the 2025 STAndards for Reporting Diagnostic accuracy studies using artificial intelligence (STARD-AI).

CONCLUSIONS: The checklist of essential reporting items will assist the systematic development of Model 1b APS by various statistical or simulation models and ensure that the Model 1b APS are scientifically valid, robust and transferable across different settings and applications in health care.

articles.title: Quantum fluctuation-driven transport crossover between two liquid states in distinguishable helium-4.
articles.abstract: We show the emergence of a quantum fluctuation-driven transport crossover between two liquid states in distinguishable helium-4 obeying Boltzmann statistics, in the absence of atomic exchange. Using path integral centroid molecular dynamics simulations over 0.1-3.3 K and 1-60 bars, we investigate the transport properties of two distinct liquid states: the low quantum dispersion liquid (LQDL) and the high quantum dispersion liquid (HQDL). While LQDL exhibits conventional liquid behavior consistent with the Stokes-Einstein (SE) relation, HQDL emerges at lower temperatures and displays anomalous gas-like transport characterized by superdiffusion and ultralow viscosity, accompanied by a breakdown of the SE relation. This counterintuitive emergence of gas-like dynamics upon cooling reflects the dominant role of nuclear quantum fluctuations, in contrast to thermal fluctuations at higher temperatures. Across the LQDL-HQDL boundary, we identify a transport crossover marked by a qualitative change in the velocity autocorrelation function (VAF), a transition in the Prandtl number, and the emergence of transport minima in shear and kinematic viscosities, thermal conductivity, and thermal diffusivity. These minima reflect a crossover from liquid-like to gas-like transport upon cooling in the low-temperature subcritical region, in addition to the universal transport minima observed in the supercritical regime. The transition from oscillatory to monotonic VAF defines a second Frenkel line, distinct from the conventional Frenkel line observed in the supercritical region. LQDL is a heat-transport-dominated dissipative fluid, whereas HQDL is a momentum-dominated inertial fluid. These results demonstrate that nuclear quantum fluctuations alone induce gas-like liquid behavior and provide a unified picture of transport phenomena in distinguishable helium-4 without superfluidity.

articles.title: Intracavity photon statistics from correlated molecular electronic structure.
articles.abstract: Quantum optics characterizes light through photon correlations, motivating their connection to correlated ab initio molecular electronic structure. In this study, intracavity photon statistics of cavity-coupled molecules are computed from QED coupled-cluster (QED-CCSD-22) densities and validated against exact diagonalization of the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian. A change of coordinate origin or dipole convention displaces the ground state coherently, so second-order and higher cumulants of the cavity field are independent of these conventions even for molecular ions. The photon subsystem of QED Hartree-Fock is exactly coherent, so the invariant statistics describe fluctuations beyond this electron-photon product reference. The field fluctuations are super-Poissonian, and their degree of second-order coherence depends primarily on cavity frequency in the tested weak-coupling regime, falling from 18.5 to 4.9 for H2 as the cavity is detuned from 5 to 20 eV. The third cumulant identifies non-Gaussian fluctuations and changes sign under reversal of the coupling direction.

articles.title: Casimir force screening by a quantum Boltzmann plasma.
articles.abstract: We develop a finite-temperature field-theoretical description of the Casimir interaction between two perfectly conducting boundaries with the intervening gap filled by a two-component quantum Boltzmann plasma embedded in a homogeneous dielectric background. The quantum motion of the charged particles is represented by imaginary-time worldlines, while the electromagnetic field is treated in the Gaussian approximation. The resulting partition function contains distinct longitudinal and transverse response contributions and an additional quantum-induced source term with no classical counterpart. In the classical limit, the theory reduces to the usual Casimir-screening picture: the static longitudinal mode is Debye screened, whereas the transverse electromagnetic sector is unaffected by classical mobile charges. Finite thermal de Broglie wavelengths modify the nonzero Matsubara response and produce the leading quantum correction to the force. In the static long-wavelength limit, the longitudinal dielectric function has, through the leading quantum correction, the same expansion structure as the Lindhard response of a degenerate electron gas under the correspondence kTF ↔ κD and kF↔λdB-1. In contrast, the static transverse response reproduces the leading high-temperature Landau orbital diamagnetic susceptibility. We investigate the crossover between classical and quantum plasma behavior in a regime where these corrections become appreciable while the plasma remains approximately nondegenerate and can still be treated, at leading order, within Maxwell-Boltzmann statistics. We illustrate this crossover for a weakly coupled electron-proton plasma and an effective Li+-solvated-electron plasma in liquid ammonia. The latter yields a sub-percent quantum correction to the force gradient for the parameters considered.

articles.title: Enhanced diffusion sampling: Efficient rare event sampling and free energy calculation with diffusion models.
articles.abstract: The rare-event sampling problem has long been the central limiting factor in molecular dynamics, especially in biomolecular simulation. Recently, diffusion models such as BioEmu have emerged as powerful equilibrium samplers that generate independent samples from complex molecular distributions, eliminating the cost of sampling rare transition events. However, a sampling problem remains when computing observables that rely on states which are rare in equilibrium, for example, folding free energies. Here, we introduce enhanced diffusion sampling, enabling efficient exploration of rare-event regions while preserving unbiased thermodynamic estimators. The key idea is to perform quantitatively accurate steering protocols to generate biased ensembles and subsequently recover equilibrium statistics via exact reweighting. We instantiate our framework in three algorithms: UmbrellaDiff (umbrella sampling with diffusion models), MetaDiff (a batchwise analog for metadynamics), and ΔG-Diff (free-energy differences via tilted ensembles). We demonstrate the three methods on toy free-energy landscapes and apply ΔG-Diff to protein folding free-energy calculations with BioEmu. Our methods reduce the cost of rare-state estimation, enabling protein folding free-energy calculations in minutes to hours of graphics processing unit time per system.

articles.title: A Comprehensive Review of PET Chemical Depolymerization: Mechanisms, Catalyst Design, and Process Intensification Toward Closed-Loop Recycling.
articles.abstract: The massive accumulation of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) waste necessitates efficient recycling technologies to mitigate environmental pollution. Chemical depolymerization converts PET into high-purity monomers, offering a promising route for closed-loop plastic circularity. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in catalytic PET depolymerization, emphasizing reaction mechanisms, catalyst design, and process intensification. We analyze major depolymerization routes, namely hydrolysis, methanolysis, glycolysis, and aminolysis while highlighting fundamental mechanistic insights such as nucleophilic transesterification and emerging β-cleavage pathways. Furthermore, we evaluate catalyst design principles for active sites (e.g., Brønsted and Lewis acids, bridged bimetallic centers, and defect-engineered structures) across various homogeneous and heterogeneous systems, including ionic liquids, metal-organic frameworks, and zeolites. Finally, we highlight recent progress in process intensification strategies, such as interfacial catalysis, microwave-assisted reactions, and tandem one-pot processes. By integrating mechanistic understanding with catalyst engineering, this review provides a comprehensive perspective and outlines future directions for sustainable, industrially viable closed-loop PET recycling.

articles.title: From Dysbiosis to Disease: How Vaginal Microbiota Shape Group B Streptococcus Pathogenesis.
articles.journal: Chembiochem : a European journal of chemical biology
articles.abstract: Host-microbe interactions refer to the dynamic relationships between hosts, such as humans, and the microorganisms present on or inside them. These associations can be beneficial, like gut bacteria facilitating digestion, or harmful, such as pathogens leading to disease. This review focuses on the reproductive tract, specifically the vaginal microbiome. Typically, a healthy vaginal microbiome is dominated by Lactobacillus species, which help protect against infections by pathogens. Dysbiosis, or a microbial imbalance, allows pathogens to invade. One such pathogen is Streptococcus agalactiae (group B Streptococcus, GBS), which can colonize the vaginal microbiome and cause infections. GBS infection during pregnancy is particularly concerning and is a major cause of adverse pregnancy outcomes. This review will explore host-microbe interactions in the vaginal microbiome, with an emphasis on GBS infection, its virulence, and current treatment strategies.

articles.title: Transcriptional control of autophagy: mechanisms, dynamics, and pharmacological modulation.
articles.abstract: The network of transcription factors (TFs) is an integral component of executing macroautophagy/autophagy-lysosome gene expression to maintain cellular homeostasis. Across metazoans, conserved TFs, particularly the helix-loop-helix factor TFEB, convert upstream signals into specific genetic programs through mechanisms ranging from DNA recognition and chromatin remodeling to biomolecular condensates. The dysregulation of TF-governed gene programming disrupts the progression of metabolic disease and cancer, highlighting that dissection of transcriptional regulation makes it a promising therapeutic target. Consequently, instead of indirectly modulating the pathways in which they are involved, targeting these essential TFs directly is becoming a new trend for pharmaceutical development. In this review, we systematically elucidate current mechanisms of the TF-driven autophagic transcriptome, and summarize current small molecules targeting these TFs in various disease.Abbreviations: AD: Alzheimer disease; articles.title: Bilingua-DPP-IV: A Bimodal Fusion Convolutional Neural Network Model for Prediction of Dipeptidyl Peptidase IV Inhibitory Peptides.
articles.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Dipeptidyl peptidase IV (DPP-IV) is a key therapeutic target for type 2 diabetes, and its inhibitory peptides are a promising class of therapeutic agents. However, the discovery of these promising drugs has been restricted, as many existing computational predictors are based on datasets that have remained static for several years.

RESULTS: Here, we first presented a newly curated and expanded benchmark dataset, then introduced Bilingua-DPP-IV, a bimodal deep learning framework that integrates features from both amino acid sequences and molecular structures. Our approach leveraged embeddings from the large-scale pretrained models ESM C and Uni-Mol2, processed through a convolutional neural network with an optimized gated fusion mechanism. On an independent test set, the Bilingua-DPP-IV ensemble model achieved a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.764 and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.963. On an external validation set, the model also demonstrated an accuracy of 0.898, exceeding the performance of existing state-of-the-art predictors, such as StructuralDPPIV.

articles.title: Designing for success in early-phase hemophilia clinical trials: historical lessons and emerging principles for next-generation therapeutics.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Hemophilia drug development has progressed through five therapeutic eras: plasma-derived concentrates, recombinant proteins, extended-half-life molecules, non-factor rebalancing agents, and gene therapy. Each transition depended not only on molecular innovation but also on early-phase trials that addressed critical translational and safety questions before pivotal testing.

AREAS COVERED: This review examines the evolution of early-phase hemophilia trial design across these five eras, identifies lessons from successful and unsuccessful programs, and proposes a ten-domain framework encompassing translational science, population selection, dose-finding, endpoints, biomarkers, laboratory standardization, immunogenicity, safety, statistics, and regulatory strategy. The framework is applied to genome editing, RNA therapeutics, rebalancing agents, and synthetic coagulation proteins, drawing on published evidence through mid-2026 and the author's experience as a clinical trial investigator.

EXPERT OPINION: Therapeutic success requires both molecular innovation and rigorous early-phase trial design. An ingenious product cannot compensate for failure to define its therapeutic window, clinically meaningful benefit, or implementation requirements. Experience with non-factor and gene therapies shows that mechanisms with compelling preclinical rationale may fail, cause harm, or remain clinically underused when durability, immunogenicity, and real-world implementation are treated as late-stage considerations. Addressing these issues from first-in-human studies will determine which emerging genome-editing and RNA-based candidates succeed.

articles.title: A fuzzy-enhanced broad learning framework with minority-class ensemble for ECG arrhythmia classification.
articles.abstract: Existing broad learning system (BLS)-based Electrocardiogram (ECG) arrhythmia classification methods still face limitations in multi-source feature representation, sample reliability modeling, and minority-class recognition. To address these issues, this study proposes a combinational improvement framework built upon BLS, integrating uncertainty-aware gated fuzzy feature enhancement and a minority-class ensemble strategy for ECG arrhythmia classification. First, heartbeat waveform, QRS complex structural information, and RR rhythm features are integrated to construct a hybrid ECG representation that jointly captures morphological and rhythm characteristics. The BLS is then employed for high-dimensional nonlinear feature mapping, upon which an uncertainty-aware gated fuzzy enhancement mechanism evaluates sample reliability through robust class prototype estimation and fuzzy membership calculation. A confidence-based gating strategy is further introduced to achieve adaptive feature enhancement, strengthening discriminative information from reliable samples while reducing noise interference caused by ambiguous boundary samples. Finally, a minority-class-aware ensemble classification strategy is developed, which employs extreme gradient boosting as the primary classifier. One-versus-rest classifiers, a complementary logistic regression model, and class-wise probability calibration are incorporated to refine classification decisions and alleviate majority-class bias caused by class imbalance. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves overall accuracies of 99.04% and 92.58% (Macro-F1 of 93.39% and 61.60%) under the intra-patient and inter-patient evaluation protocols, respectively. The framework trades a moderate training-time and memory footprint (an ensemble of tree models over analysis of variance-selected BLS features) for these minority-class gains, while inference remains a CPU-friendly single forward pass through the frozen pipeline. It improves minority-class recognition relative to the compared methods under severe class imbalance, while the recognition of fusion beats under the inter-patient protocol remains challenging (five-seed meanF1 of 6.722.69%) and is explicitly discussed as a limitation.

articles.title: easyPET.3D measurement of positron emitter maps in proton-irradiated PMMA phantoms.
articles.abstract: Accurate range verification is a critical component of proton therapy, ensuring that the high dose gradients characteristic of Bragg peaks are delivered precisely to the target volume. This work presents the first experimental evaluation of the easyPET.3D, a compact and cost-effective preclinical positron emission tomography scanner, as a potential tool for quality control assessment. Homogeneous PMMA phantoms were irradiated at the Paul Scherrer Institute Gantry 1 facility using proton beam energies ranging from 138 MeV-195 MeV. The resulting 3Dactivity distributions were reconstructed and analyzed to assess the system's spatial accuracy, stability, and sensitivity. For the intermediate energy of 160 MeV, the measured activity profile showed a high degree of agreement with Monte Carlo (GATE) simulations, with a difference of 0.24 mm in theposition. The system exhibited robust performance under varying irradiation conditions. Doubling the number of delivered protons relative to a clinically relevant value resulted in a deviation of only 0.4 mm in the calculated range, confirming the method's reproducibility. Furthermore, the system successfully resolved distinct beam paths in a dual-energy irradiation mode, distinguishing tracks separated vertically by 10 mm and quantifying longitudinal range differences. Sensitivity tests indicated that the system is capable of detecting longitudinal phantom displacements as small as 1 mm. The relationship between expected and measured displacements followed a linear trend with a slope of 1.13, indicating a systematic overestimation of 13%, and an offset of 0.45 mm, reflecting a small baseline bias. While further optimization of detector sensitivity and reconstruction algorithms is required to reduce acquisition times for routine clinical workflows, these findings validate the potential of easyPET.3D as a promising, accessible solution for proton range verification.

articles.title: Antimony-Doped Violet Phosphorus Nanosheets: Band Gap Engineering for Enhanced Photodynamic Effect and Efficient Antibacterial Activity.
articles.abstract: Bacterial infections pose a severe threat to public health worldwide, and overuse of traditional antibiotics induces bacterial resistance, limiting the efficacy of conventional therapies. Two-dimensional violet phosphorus nanosheets (VPNS) have emerged as promising photodynamic antibacterial materials owing to their unique layered structure and light-responsive capability. However, the inherent wide band gap of VPNS restricts photogenerated electron transition and reactive oxygen species production, resulting in unsatisfactory photodynamic therapy efficiency, which severely hinders their biomedical applications. To address these limitations, a facile antimony (Sb) doping strategy is developed to modulate the electronic band structure of VPNS for significantly boosted photodynamic antibacterial performance. As a congener of phosphorus, Sb possesses excellent optical and electrical properties, which can effectively optimize the photoelectric characteristics of VPNS. Results confirm that Sb doping narrows the band gap of VPNS from 1.91 to 1.42 eV and boosts reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation by 2.3-fold. In mouse skin wound infection models, Sb-doped VPNS (VPSb) achieves remarkable therapeutic efficacy against Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) infection and accelerates wound healing at a low concentration of 0.1 mg/mL. The optimized VPSb, with its excellent therapeutic performance, demonstrates great application prospects for clinical bacterial wound infection therapy.

articles.title: A Dual pH‑Responsive Hydrogel with Site‑Specific Therapeutic Functions for Differential Pathological Microenvironment Remodeling and Accelerated Repair of Infected Diabetic Wounds.
articles.abstract: Diabetic skin wounds have disrupted local acid-base balance, prone to bacterial adhesion and sustained chronic inflammation that hinders tissue repair. Benefiting from the unique properties of oxidized sodium alginate, we prepared a dual pH-responsive Schiff base crosslinked hydrogel loaded with herbal nanoparticles to remodel the defective wound microenvironment and speed up regeneration. Dynamic covalent crosslinking endows the hydrogel with favorable flexibility and shape adaptability to fit irregular wound surfaces. It exhibits obvious dual pH sensitivity: strong antibacterial activity in bacteria-rich acidic niches and slow hydrolysis under diabetic wound alkalinity, achieving stable drug release without burst leakage. The encapsulated nanoparticles exhibit multiple complementary functions. Zn2+ acts as an efficient bactericide to eliminate pathogens. L-Arginine facilitates nitric oxide (NO) generation to promote angiogenesis and M2 macrophage polarization. The glycyrrhetinic acid-2-hydroxyacetophenone conjugate (GA-HAP) suppresses proinflammatory cytokines to relieve local inflammation. In vitro and in vivo experiments verify that this composite hydrogel balances wound pH, eradicates bacterial infection, and mitigates persistent inflammation, remarkably accelerating diabetic wound healing. This pH-sensitive herbal hydrogel holds great potential for microenvironment regulation and clinical therapy of intractable diabetic wounds.

articles.title: Dual-Responsive Nanoplatform: In Situ Self-Assembly Enables OFF-to-ON Photothermal Switching for Multimodal Synergistic Tumor Therapy.
articles.abstract: Photothermal therapy has attracted extensive attention in tumor treatment owing to its spatiotemporal controllability and noninvasiveness. However, the nonselective "always on" nature of traditional photothermal nanoagents together with the intrinsic thermal resistance within tumor cells has hampered the therapeutic efficacy. Herein, we developed a tumor-microenvironment-responsive transformable prenanotherapeutic platform with a polyethyleneimine (PEI)-coated tannic acid-Ca2+ chelate core and an outer shell of Fe2+-doped ZIF-90, which enabled the in situ generation of photothermal agents, synchronous activation of multiple therapeutic modalities, as well as cascaded synergistic enhancement of antitumor potency. First, degradation triggered by high-concentration adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and mild acidity within tumor cells liberated Fe2+ to catalyze hydroxyl radical (·OH) production for chemodynamic therapy. Meanwhile, the generated Fe3+ readily underwent in situ self-assembly with tannic acid to form photothermal agents, which competitively released Ca2+ and induced calcium overload. Subsequently, the dual mitochondrial destruction pathway induced by ·OH and excess Ca2+ suppressed ATP synthesis, which further downregulated the expression of heat shock protein 70 and elevated tumor cell thermosensitivity to realize mild photothermal therapy. Moreover, heat generated via photothermal agents enhanced the efficiency of Fenton-like reactions for robust ·OH accumulation, further improving the therapeutic efficacy. In vitro experiments revealed the underlying synergistic antitumor mechanism, while in vivo experiments confirmed the remarkable tumor suppression capacity of the nanomaterial. Notably, an intelligent TME-responsive "OFF-to-ON" multifunctional nanoplatform was fabricated on the basis of differential binding affinities of metal ions and polyphenols, offering a safer, more efficient and precise strategy for synergistic cancer therapy.

articles.title: Patient and database shift in lightweight ECG arrhythmia classification: a controlled evaluation of noise, quantization, and embedded inference.
articles.abstract: Efficient microcontroller execution does not ensure reliable electrocardiogram classification across patients and databases. We conducted a controlled benchmark of three convolutional architectures under a corrected subject-disjoint MIT-BIH split, external INCART testing, noise stress test database artifacts, 16-bit floating-point (FP16) and full-integer 8-bit (INT8) conversion, and classifier-only invocation on an ESP32 without external RAM. Five fixed seeds were used. On the MIT-BIH test cohort (DS2), INT8 four-class macro-F1 was 0.474-0.498 and supraventricular (S) recall was 0.150-0.180. Mean S-class area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was below 0.5 in all six architecture-regime groups, although all corresponding record-cluster intervals included 0.5. Within-record ranking could remain high despite poor pooled ranking. On INCART, S-class ranking was stronger, with all six patient-cluster AUROC intervals above 0.5, but the representative mixed-noise depthwise-separable convolutional neural network (DS-CNN) achieved 0.797 recall with 0.074 precision. Including record 201, which shares a subject with test record 202, increased DS2 S-recall point estimates by 2.49-14.68 percentage points. In the primary architecture panel, FP16 and INT8 met the engineering tolerances in all 120 comparisons. DS-CNN required 9.49 ms per classifier invocation on the ESP32 using preprocessed, annotation-centered inputs. Acquisition, QRS detection, preprocessing, current, and energy were not measured. Patient-dependentS-score behavior and external false-positive predictions limited this panel more than numerical precision or microcontroller resources.

articles.title: Paintable In Situ Gelling Bioelectronic Interfaces for Epidermal Electrophysiological Monitoring.
articles.abstract: Noninvasive epidermal electrophysiological monitoring is frequently constrained by unstable electrode-skin contact interfaces over soft, textured, and dynamically deforming skin. The predefined geometries of conventional electrodes limit their capacity to conform to local microtopography. Here, we introduce an in situ gelation strategy performed directly on the epidermis to construct a conformal ionic bioelectronic interface. A fluidic precursor comprising gelatin and tannic acid is initially stabilized against premature gelation via competitive solvent-solute interactions. Upon application, solvent evaporation and gelatin reassembly induce rapid network formation. This process directly yields a highly conformal and gently detachable interface with remarkably low contact impedance. The resulting hydrated dynamic network provides mechanical compliance, robust interfacial adhesion, stretch-tolerant ionic conduction, and cooling-induced interfacial weakening that enables gentle removal. The on-skin-gelled interface reduces skin-electrode contact impedance to 30 kΩ at 10 Hz, compared with 191 kΩ for commercial conductive pastes, and increases the signal-to-noise ratio from 24.9 to 27.8 dB. In proof-of-concept demonstrations, the interface supports within-subject electromyography-based gesture recognition with a classification accuracy of 93.4% and electroencephalography recordings of eye-state-dependent α-rhythm modulation as well as short-term sleep-related waveforms. These findings underscore the potential of on-skin in situ gelation as a versatile approach to fabricating paintable ionic bioelectronic interfaces for advanced electrophysiological monitoring.

articles.title: A harmonisation framework for multi-centre preclinical PET imaging across a national research infrastructure.
articles.abstract: Objective.Quantitative preclinical positron emission tomography (PET) imaging plays an important role in translational research, yet variability across scanners, sites, and analysis workflows remains a major barrier to robust multi-centre studies. In this work, we developed and evaluated a harmonisation framework across a national network of preclinical PET facilities.Approach.Six identical National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA) NU 4-2008 image quality phantoms were manufactured and distributed to six sites, where they were imaged using local acquisition and reconstruction protocols across multiple scanner platforms.Main Results.Substantial variability in contrast recovery, uniformity, and spill-over ratios was observed under site-specific conditions. Centralised automated re-analysis produced only minor reductions in variability, indicating that inter-user effects were relatively small, compared to site-specific protocol variations. In contrast, optimisation of reconstruction parameters led to a marked reduction in inter-scanner variability (an average of 60% reduction across larger rods), particularly for voxel-wise maximum contrast recovery coefficients (CRC), which are more sensitive to noise and reconstruction settings than the standard axial averaging NEMA CRC metric. Following harmonisation, the variability of CRCapproached and was lower that of conventional axial-averaged NEMA analysis (CRC), with reductions ranging 7%-33% across the 1-5 mm rods, demonstrating improved quantitative consistency even at the voxel level.Significance.These findings show that scanner and site-specific protocol variations are the dominant factors for harmonisation in preclinical PET. By systematically evaluating acquisition, image reconstruction and analysis related sources of variability across a national network of heterogeneous preclinical PET systems, this work provides a practical framework for harmonisation. The proposed framework is conceptually aligned with clinical harmonisation initiatives such as EARL and provides a practical basis for the future development of harmonised performance ranges across preclinical scanners. This enables more reliable multi-centre studies and supports the use of quantitative, voxel-wise imaging biomarkers in translational research.

articles.title: Heterologous expression of the Metarhizium anisopliae barc gene cluster reveals a diphenyl ether-to-xanthene transformation in barceloneic acid biosynthesis.
articles.abstract: Filamentous fungi generate chemical diversity through several evolutionary strategies, including the elaboration of conserved biosynthetic intermediates into structurally distinct secondary metabolites. Emodin and its corresponding anthrone are central intermediates in fungal aromatic polyketide metabolism, yet the enzymatic logic that remodels these precursors into more complex scaffolds remains incompletely understood. To investigate this process, we examined an infection-responsive non-reducing polyketide synthase biosynthetic gene cluster (barc) from the entomopathogenic fungus Metarhizium anisopliae predicted to encode an emodin-derived aromatic polyketide pathway. Heterologous reconstruction of the barc cluster in Aspergillus nidulans led to the production of the previously reported diphenyl ether barceloneic acid A (1) and the xanthene barceloneic acid C2 (2), together with two new compounds derived from 2, barceloneic acids D and E (3 and 4). Compound 3 is a cyclopentanone adduct of the xanthene 2, whereas 4 is a polyketide-indole hybrid, highlighting the chemical reactivity of the xanthene 2 scaffold. Through combinatorial heterologous expression and feeding assays, we identified a predicted glucose-methanol-choline oxidoreductase (BarcL) as the enzyme responsible for converting diphenyl ether 1 to xanthene 2. This defines a previously uncharacterised oxidative scaffold-remodelling step in barceloneic acid biosynthesis, revealing how an emodin-derived pathway can access a xanthene scaffold. Deletion of the backbone gene barcB in M. anisopliae did not significantly alter virulence towards Tenebrio molitor (mealworm) under the conditions tested, suggesting that barceloneic acids are not essential for pathogenicity in this insect model.

articles.title: Algebraic multicomponent fluorescence lifetime estimation from harmonic phase measurements under two-photon excitation.
articles.abstract: We formulate and numerically evaluate a direct, non-iterative algebraic estimator for multicomponent fluorescence lifetimes using harmonic phase measurements in a two-photon excitation scheme. The method operates on the complex harmonic responses available at the repetition frequency of a femtosecond pulse train and its harmonics. Rather than performing iterative nonlinear lifetime fitting, we map the measured harmonic responses through a linear coefficient-reconstruction step to the denominator polynomial of a rational representation of the multiexponential decay and obtain the decay constants from its roots. This procedure requires neither initial lifetime estimates nor iterative nonlinear minimization. Numerical simulations were performed for a three-component system, with photon-limited performance evaluated using Poisson counting statistics. For the closely spaced lifetime set of 0.5, 1.5, and 2.5 ns, the mean relative lifetime error decreased from 14.49% at a peak expected count of 100 photons per time bin to 5.94% at 1000 photons and 1.31% at 10 000 photons, with each condition evaluated by averaging 500 statistically independent acquisitions. In a matched 500-trial Monte Carlo comparison atexpected photons per pixel, the success probabilities were 0.484 for the unconstrained algebraic estimator, 0.854 for the DC-constrained algebraic estimator, and 0.898 for single-start nonlinear least-squares (NLLS). Thus, imposing the DC constraint substantially improved the photon-noise robustness of the algebraic reconstruction relative to the minimally determined unconstrained formulation, while single-start NLLS remained slightly more robust than the DC-constrained algebraic estimator. In a separate matched 500-sample computational benchmark atexpected photons per pixel, the median parameter-estimation times were 0.138, 0.095, and 5.552 ms per pixel for the unconstrained algebraic, DC-constrained algebraic, and single-start NLLS estimators, respectively. Relative to the DC-constrained algebraic median, the unconstrained algebraic and single-start NLLS calculations required approximately 1.45 and 58.35 times longer processing time, respectively. These results identify both a constraint-induced robustness improvement within the algebraic formulation and a robustness-computation trade-off relative to iterative fitting. The present work should therefore be regarded as a theoretical and numerical algebraic implementation within the established multifrequency frequency-domain framework. Experimental validation and harmonic-dependent instrument-response calibration remain necessary for practical two-photon FLIM implementation.

articles.title: Development of a bioadhesive hydrogel with antioxidant activity for enhanced diabetic wound healing.
articles.abstract: Diabetic chronic wounds which often lead to amputation remain a significant unresolved challenge in clinical practice, posing serious risks to patient health and survival. Existing clinical treatments such as topical administration, traditional dressings and debridement are often inadequate to address the complex pathological microenvironment (chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, etc.) of diabetic chronic wounds, resulting in long treatment cycles and poor outcomes for patients. To address the key pathological factors that impede wound healing, a functional hydrogel dressing was developed in this study using natural polyphenol tannic acid (TA) and biocompatible polyvinyl alcohol (PVA), and aldehyde phenylboronic acid (FPBA) and cyanophenylboronic acid (CPBA) as small molecule crosslinkers. The polyphenol-based hydrogel exhibited strong tissue adhesion, ensuring stable adherence to the wound site after application, thereby preventing infection and mechanical re-injury. And the G-PT hydrogel loaded with TA markedly reduced reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and effectively inhibited DNA damage. Meanwhile, they reduced the levels of early inflammatory factors IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF-α, promoted the polarization of macrophages toward an anti-inflammatory phenotype. In vitro and in vivo evaluations demonstrated that the hydrogel significantly promoted the healing of both acute skin incisions and chronic diabetic wounds by mitigating oxidative stress and regulating macrophage polarization. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of this multifunctional hydrogel dressing as a promising strategy for treating diabetic wounds.

articles.title: Biomimetic multilayer small-diameter vascular grafts with tunable mechanical behavior.
articles.abstract: Small-diameter vascular grafts remain limited by thrombosis, intimal hyperplasia, and inadequate mechanical and biological integration, motivating manufacturing strategies that can simultaneously control tubular architecture, mechanical response, and the blood-contacting interface. Herein, we report a bioinspired coaxial dry-jet wet-spinning platform using a custom-engineered three-channel spinneret to continuously fabricate bilayer thermoplastic polyurethane/polylactic acid (TPU/PLA) hollow constructs with an external TPU layer, a luminal PLA layer, and a sacrificial water core. Rheological screening identified compatible TPU/PLA processing windows, while systematic variation of polymer and bore-fluid injection rates enabled regulation of wall geometry and axial mechanical properties. The higher-solids 18T22P formulation consistently exhibited greater tensile and dynamic stiffness than 14T18P, and the construct fabricated at 1.0 mL min-1 provided a balanced response with an ultimate tensile strength of 5.84 ± 0.69 MPa, Young's modulus of 171.51 ± 23.85 MPa, and storage modulus of 190.36 MPa at 37 °C. Following 14 days of PBS conditioning, mass loss remained below 1%, although tensile-strength and modulus retention decreased to approximately 51% and 55%, respectively. Plasma activation followed by type I collagen coating increased surface wettability, with a 4 h coating condition maximizing NIH/3T3 attachment. The collagen-functionalized PLA lumen supported enhanced HUVEC attachment and maintained short-term endothelial metabolic activity comparable to a collagen control. Both polymer interfaces exhibited negligible hemolytic responses, comparable platelet adhesion, and delayed whole-blood clot development relative to the blank condition. Collectively, this work establishes a process-structure-property-biointerface framework for continuously manufactured multilayer hollow constructs with tunable mechanics and favorable preliminary vascular-cell and blood compatibility.

articles.title: Manipulation of the cell cycle by HIV-1.
articles.abstract: Many viruses manipulate the host cell cycle to enhance viral replication and promote their evasion of host immune defenses. Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) is no exception and triggers cell cycle arrest during its infection of replicating CD4+ T cells, acting predominantly through the activities of the viral proteins Vpr and Vif. Here, we summarize HIV-1's effects on cell cycle regulation, focusing on the distinct mechanisms that underpin Vpr and Vif's modulation of cell cycle checkpoints. We also discuss how these activities, when combined, may help the virus to enhance replication and promote reactivation from long-term latency-the major barrier to a cure for HIV/AIDS. A deeper understanding of how HIV-1 remodels the host cell cycle should reveal important new cell biology and may inform the development of therapeutic strategies relevant to curative interventions.

articles.title: Biodistribution and dosimetry of free118Te, anin vivogenerator of the positron emitter118Sb for long-term positron emission tomography.
articles.abstract: Objective. Tellurium-118 (118Te;t1/2= 6.00 ± 0.02 d) can act as anin vivogenerator of the positron emitter antimony-118 (118Sb;t1/2= 3.6 ± 0.3 min), enabling positron emission tomography (PET) over a week or longer. This work assessed absorbed doses associated with free118Te to establish a dosimetric safety basis for118Te radiopharmaceuticals.Approach. Injection solutions of free118Te were prepared by alpha-particle irradiation of an enriched tin-116 target followed by radiochemical isolation.Ex vivobiodistribution in healthy female Slc:ICR mice was acquired at seven time points from 2 h to 29 d postinjection (n= 6 per time point). Time-integrated activity coefficients were computed from the biodistribution profiles and extrapolated to a human model using relative mass scaling. Absorbed dose coefficients (ADCs) were calculated following the medical internal radiation dose formalism with computational phantoms implemented in the dosimetry software OLINDA. Dosimetric contributions from118Te and its coproduced radioisotopic impurity119mTe (t1/2= 4.69 ± 0.04 d), along with their equilibrium daughters118Sb and119Sb, were individually assessed.Main results. The kidneys exhibited the highest ADC in both mouse (2666.0 mGy MBq-1) and human (2.639 mGy MBq-1) models. Bone received the second-highest ADC in the mouse model, 1855.5 mGy MBq-1. Antimony-118 dominated absorbed doses across all organs examined, accounting for more than 82% of ADCs in both models. Contributions from118Te,119mTe, and119Sb were minor by comparison.Significance. The kidneys and bone were identified as the primary dosimetric targets of free118Te, with its daughter118Sb being the principal dose contributor. The limited dosimetric impact from118Te provides justification for its use as anin vivogenerator of118Sb for long-term PET. The ADCs reported here offer a quantitative basis for assessing the dosimetric safety of118Te radiopharmaceuticals.

articles.title: Individual Differences in Dopaminergic Modulation of Exploration-Exploitation Behavior.
articles.journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
articles.abstract: Dopamine (DA) has been implicated in exploration-exploitation behavior, i.e., exploring novel, potentially better options versus exploiting known, previously rewarding options. Impairments in this trade-off occur in psychiatric disorders involving DAergic dysfunction, including addiction and schizophrenia. Pharmacological studies revealed a contribution of DA to exploration, but inconsistent findings suggest interindividual variability in baseline DA may modulate effects. To address this, we investigated the effects of the DA precursor L-DOPA on exploration-exploitation during reinforcement learning in N = 75 healthy participants (n = 32 women), following a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, preregistered design (https://osf.io/p2r7u). We assessed whether putative baseline DA markers, including spontaneous eyeblink rate, working memory (WM) capacity, and impulsivity, modulated drug effects and examined visual fixation patterns and pupil dilation. L-DOPA had no overall effect on computational model parameters of random exploration, directed exploration or choice perseveration. WM capacity moderated drug effects on random exploration, with stronger effects at higher WM capacity. Remaining DA proxies showed no credible effects. Pooling male participant data with that from an earlier male-only study (Chakroun et al., 2020; total N = 74), L-DOPA increased uncertainty-dependent value weighting and perseveration strength. No credible drug effects were observed in female participants. Pupil dilation was tonically increased under L-DOPA and scaled with exploration behavior and prediction error, confirming that pupillometry can index exploration dynamics. Visual exploration patterns reflected uncertainty-driven sampling but were unaffected by L-DOPA. Results suggest that DAergic modulation of exploration and perseveration may be contingent on cognitive capacity and sex, rather than exerting uniform effects.

articles.title: What's new in heart failure? September 2026.
Medical leadership between motivation and organisational support: findings from a contemporary survey.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Medical leadership is essential for high-value care, yet organisational conditions remain variable. This study aims to examine whether clinicians' motivation and perceived readiness to lead are matched by enabling infrastructures (e.g. protected time, decision support and shared-governance routines) and how gaps relate to perceived impact and clinician wellbeing.

DESIGN/METHODOLOGY/APPROACH: The authors conducted an anonymous, cross-sectional online survey distributed internationally via professional networks and snowball sampling. Descriptive analyses compared clinicians and non-clinician leaders on five-point Likert items. Exploratory models assessed associations between cumulative "support deficits", perceived leadership impact and stress/burnout. In addition, a Shared-Governance Alignment Index was constructed. The survey was open from 4 November 2025 to 17 December 2025 and eligible respondents were clinicians or non-clinician healthcare leaders able to report on leadership, organisational support or clinician-administrator collaboration within their healthcare setting.

FINDINGS: A total of 143 responses were analysed (107 clinicians; 36 non-clinician leaders), predominantly from Italy (76%). Clinicians reported strong interest in leadership roles [median 5 (4-5); 88% agree/strongly agree] and high self-rated preparedness [median 4 (4-5); 80% agree/strongly agree], but limited organisational supports, particularly protected time for leadership/quality improvement [median 2 (1-3)] and constrained access to decision support tools [median 3 (2-4)]. Increasing cumulative support deficits showed a dose-response relationship with lower perceived leadership impact (e.g. endorsement that leadership improves care quality: 94% with 0 deficits versus 53% with 2 deficits) and higher odds of stress/burnout. Clinicians also rated shared-governance conditions less favourably than non-clinician leaders, indicating persistent perceptual misalignment in clinician-administrator collaboration.

RESEARCH LIMITATIONS/IMPLICATIONS: This study used a voluntary, cross-sectional survey, limiting causal inference and increasing susceptibility to self-selection, common method and social desirability biases. Measures relied on self-report rather than objective indicators of governance quality, decision-support availability or performance outcomes. The international, network-based sampling may under-represent some regions, specialties and non-clinician perspectives. Nonetheless, findings generate testable propositions for longitudinal and mixed-methods research examining how protected time, shared-governance routines and decision-support infrastructure influence leadership effectiveness and clinician wellbeing and whether closing the motivation-support gap improves organisational outcomes. Future studies should incorporate administrative data.

PRACTICAL IMPLICATIONS: Organisations should complement leadership development with structural protections: defended time, accessible decision-support tools and clear shared-governance routines (co-owned decisions and aligned metrics). Without these supports, clinician motivation may translate into strain rather than sustained improvement.

SOCIAL IMPLICATIONS: Strengthening medical leadership through protected time, decision-support and shared governance can yield broader social benefits beyond organisational performance. When clinicians and administrators co-own improvement priorities, care processes become more reliable, reducing avoidable harm and enhancing public trust in health services. Better-supported leaders may also curb burnout and turnover, stabilising the workforce that communities depend on. More inclusive governance structures can amplify frontline and patient voices, supporting equity in service redesign and ensuring scarce resources are allocated transparently and ethically. These conditions may improve access, particularly for marginalised groups during pressures.

ORIGINALITY/VALUE: The study frames medical leadership as an organisational capability and identifies a "motivation-support gap". By associating self-reported structural deficits with perceived effectiveness and wellbeing, it offers actionable targets to strengthen clinician-administrator partnership and leadership sustainability. The revised framing also explicitly situates medical leadership within digital readiness, artificial intelligence-enabled decision support and health-information-system adoption as contemporary components of organisational support.

articles.title: Probability-Dependent Scaling of Fear Responding, But Not Unconditioned Stimulus Inflation, Requires the Periaqueductal Gray.
articles.journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
articles.abstract: Adaptive behavior requires animals to estimate threat, update these estimates following new aversive experiences, and align fear responding to up-to-date estimates. The periaqueductal gray (PAG) is traditionally viewed as a downstream relay that converts threat estimates into freezing. Here we tested whether the PAG is necessary for probability-dependent scaling of fear responding and for updating threat estimates through unconditioned stimulus inflation. We deleted neurons across the complete anterior-posterior span of the PAG using a dual-viral approach and then quantified deletion extent and subregion specificity using machine-learning methods. In Experiment 1, 40 Long-Evans rats (20 females) underwent fear discrimination in which a threat cue predicted footshock with 30 or 10% probability, while a neutral cue never predicted footshock. Ethograms revealed that control rats scaled a suite of reward, exploratory, and defensive behaviors to threat probability (threat > neutral and 30 > 10%). PAG deletion abolished scaling (threat > neutral, but 30 ≈ 10%). In Experiment 2, 40 Long-Evans rats (20 females) first received separate light conditioning and tone conditioning with a mild footshock. During unconditioned stimulus inflation, half the rats received light-intense shock pairings, while the other half received additional light-mild shock pairings.
