This platform complements electrophysiology-centred safety assessment and provides proof of concept for classification of subtle drug-induced contractile phenotypes.

articles.title: Reimagining Dental Education Summit Working Group 4: Consensus Recommendations for Structural Interprofessional Education in Dental Training.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Despite decades of attention to interprofessional education (IPE) in dental education, many programs still operationalize IPE as episodic exposure rather than as a durable, assessable competence embedded in clinical workflows. This gap limits the translation of IPE into interprofessional collaborative practice (IPCP), particularly for medically complex patients and populations most affected by fragmented care.

OBJECTIVE: To move IPE from ceremonial participation to structural integration across predoctoral dental education and clinical training environments, by developing consensus recommendations from Working Group 4 of the Reimagining Dental Education Summit (Harvard School of Dental Medicine, June 11-13, 2026).

CONSENSUS PROCESS: Working Group 4 consisted of nine dental education leaders and experts (two co-chairs, one summit scholar, and six members). Recommendations were developed using a structured "future-back" methodology in working sessions, iterative drafting, and plenary report-out. Evidence inputs included competency frameworks (IPEC), accreditation standards (CODA), staged integration frameworks, implementation tools, and exemplars of integrated care delivery (e.g., federally qualified health centers [FQHCs] and integrated health systems). Consensus was achieved through iterative discussion and a nominal group technique to reach unanimous agreement on final recommendations and proposed evaluation metrics.

RECOMMENDATIONS: The group recommends: (1) defining IPE competence as measurable, dentistry and oral health-specific outcomes; (2) prioritizing strategic partnerships beyond medicine (e.g., pharmacy, nursing, social work, nutrition, occupational/physical therapy); (3) anchoring IPE in IPCP settings such as FQHCs and integrated systems; (4) building an alumni/outcomes follow-up system to assess whether IPE training changes practice behaviors; and (5) strengthening communication and referral processes, including closed-loop referrals, even when electronic health records are not shared.

CONCLUSIONS: Structural IPE requires outcome-based performance expectations, practice-linked implementation models, and accountability mechanisms that measure behavior change and care-process improvement for both the learner and the patient, during training and after graduation. These consensus recommendations offer a practical roadmap for dental education programs, accreditors, and partners seeking to operationalize integrated oral health care.

articles.title: Kiwifruit Xylem Sap Promotes Pseudomonas syringae pv. actinidiae Proliferation and Vascular Colonization.
articles.abstract: The xylem has traditionally been considered a nutrient-poor environment, yet it is associated with systemic colonization by Pseudomonas syringae pv. actinidiae (Psa), the causal agent of kiwifruit bacterial canker. To clarify how Psa proliferates within this niche, we combined histopathology, metabolomics, bacterial growth kinetics, and gene-expression analyses. Psa exhibited a proliferation-during-migration pattern, reaching approximately 109 CFU·g-1 while traversing the vasculature at 0.24 cm·h-1 under condition of 16°C and 70% relative humidity, causing irreversible vascular necrosis. Crucially, xylem sap from Actinidia chinensis cv. 'Hongyang', in which systemic infection is readily established, and A. deliciosa cv. 'Hayward', in which systemic spread is uncommon, supported comparable ex vivo bacterial growth. Metabolomics revealed conserved pathogen-induced metabolic reprogramming, marked by targeted depletion of key carbon/nitrogen sources coupled with coordinated shifts in glycolysis-TCA flux and amino acid metabolism. A synthetic xylem medium containing 7 amino acids, 3 sugars, and 4 organic acids recapitulated high-density proliferation. Xylem sap exposure also increased the expression of selected motility- and type III secretion system-associated genes. These findings indicate that kiwifruit xylem sap provides a permissive nutritional environment and supports virulence-related traits, but does not by itself determine whether Psa becomes systemic. Cultivar differences in systemic infection are more likely associated with host defenses and pathogen containment before xylem entry.

articles.title: Functional characterization of a 3-O-sulfate tolerant heparin lyase from Bacteroides eggerthii.
articles.abstract: Heparin is a sulfated glycosaminoglycan, and the most used pharmaceutical anticoagulant worldwide. Heparin is isolated primarily from porcine sources, and possesses a complex variable structure, wherein anticoagulant activity is principally derived from the pentasaccharide GlcNS6S-GlcA-GlcNS3S6S-IdoA2S-GlcNS6S (AGA*IA) motif, containing an infrequent 3-O-sulfated glucosamine that enhances antithrombin stabilization. Pedobacter heparinus heparin lyases are currently widely employed for characterization of heparin and its derivatives, but have limited activity near regions of 3-O-sulfation, hindering analyses of anticoagulation relevant sequences. Here, using a panel of biophysical and structural techniques, we show that Bacteroides eggerthii lyase I liberates ΔUA-GlcNS3S6S disaccharides from the defined pentasaccharide, fondaparinux. This activity provides improved access to 3-O-sulfated heparin standards, with potential to aid heparin quality control.

articles.title: Progression of Tricuspid Regurgitation After Cardiac Implantable Electronic Device Implantation and Its Impact on Mortality and Hospitalization: A Single-Center Cohort Study.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Tricuspid regurgitation (TR) progression is a recognized complication of cardiac implantable electronic device (CIED) implantation, yet its prognostic impact on long-term clinical outcomes remains incompletely defined.

METHODS AND RESULTS: In this single-center retrospective cohort, 303 patients undergoing CIED implantation between 2005 and 2023 were followed for a median of 4.8 years. TR severity was assessed echocardiographically at baseline and 12 months. The primary endpoint was TR progression (≥ 1-grade worsening); secondary endpoints were all-cause mortality, cardiovascular hospitalization, their composite, and progression to severe TR, analyzed by Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression. TR progressed in 103 patients (34.0%), regressed in 33 (10.9%), and remained stable in 167 (55.1%), a net rightward shift (p < 0.001). Progression differed by device type (p = 0.031): among the larger subgroups, VVI-ICD showed the greatest net progression (31.8% worsened vs. 6.9% improved; p < 0.001) and CRT-D the highest regression (18.8%). During follow-up, 67 patients (22.1%) died and 164 (54.1%) were hospitalized. Overall TR progression was not independently associated with mortality (HR 1.118, p = 0.693) but independently predicted cardiovascular hospitalization (HR 1.640, p = 0.003) and the composite endpoint (HR 1.480, p = 0.014). On unadjusted analysis, progression specifically to severe TR (n = 15) was associated with increased mortality (HR 1.99, p = 0.024) and cardiovascular hospitalization (HR 2.45, p < 0.001).

CONCLUSION: TR progression occurs in approximately one-third of CIED recipients within the first year and independently predicts cardiovascular hospitalization. Progression to severe TR identifies a higher-risk subset, supporting routine post-implant echocardiographic surveillance.

articles.title: Different Factors Drive Initiation of Gametocytogenesis Versus Gametocyte Carriage in Plasmodium falciparum Infections.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Gametocyte carriage varies across Plasmodium falciparum infections. The extent to which this variation reflects differences in the initiation of gametocytogenesis and/or gametocyte maturation remains unclear. We investigated determinants of initiation of gametocytogenesis and gametocyte carriage in P. falciparum infections from Malawi.

METHODS: A total of 1108 P. falciparum infections from a cohort study conducted in Malawi between 2019 and 2020 underwent ccp4 and pfmget qRT-PCR to measure gametocyte carriage, ap2-g and sbp1 RT-PCR to quantify gametocytogenesis initiation in ring-stage parasites, and pfs230 DNA amplicon sequencing to estimate infection complexity. Mixed-effects logistic regression was used to evaluate predictors of gametocytogenesis initiation and gametocyte carriage, and mixed-effects linear regression was used to evaluate predictors of ap2-g gene transcript abundance and gametocyte density.

RESULTS: Gametocyte marker transcripts were detected in 54% (594/1108) of infections and ap2-g transcripts were detected in 41% (429/1047) of infections with detectable ring-stage parasites. Parasite density was positively associated with ap2-g expression, and ap2-g expression was more likely in polyclonal compared to monoclonal infections. Children <6 years old had lower ap2-g transcript abundance than adults but were more likely to carry gametocytes and have higher gametocyte density. Asymptomatic infections showed higher ap2-g transcript abundance and greater gametocyte prevalence and density than symptomatic infections.

CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that infection complexity and parasite density may play a role in the initiation of gametocytogenesis, whereas host immunity and duration of infection may play a larger role in gametocyte carriage in P. falciparum infections.

articles.title: Substance use, related harms and public health responses in Colombia: A national profile.
articles.abstract:
AIMS: To provide a comprehensive national profile of substance use patterns, drug-related harms, treatment and harm reduction responses, and policy developments in Colombia, and to analyze how public health reforms coexist with historically prohibitionist frameworks.

METHODS: We synthesized data from national household, school, and university surveys, epidemiological surveillance systems, official statistics, policy documents, and peer-reviewed research. Evidence was analyzed to describe trends in substance use, overdose and related harms, treatment access, harm reduction initiatives, and the broader legal and institutional context.

RESULTS: Alcohol, tobacco, and cannabis remain the most widely used substances in Colombia, while emerging synthetic drugs and opioid use have increased pressure on health and social services. Drug-related harms, including overdose and mental health problems, show significant regional and socioeconomic disparities. Although treatment coverage and harm reduction interventions, including community-based programs and supervised consumption services, have expanded in recent years, access remains uneven, particularly in rural and peripheral areas. Colombia's contemporary drug policy reflects a hybrid governance model in which constitutional protections of personal autonomy and recent harm reduction reforms coexist with enforcement-oriented practices shaped by illicit drug markets, armed conflict, and territorial inequality.

SUMMARY: Colombia illustrates both the opportunities and the structural constraints of public health-oriented drug policy in middle-income countries deeply embedded in transnational drug economies. Strengthening surveillance systems, expanding territorially adapted services, and integrating health policy with broader social and development strategies will be essential to consolidate more coherent and equitable responses.

articles.title: A comparative analysis of cell death signalling in RNA and DNA virus infections and potential inhibitory strategies.
articles.abstract: The recent COVID-19 pandemic and the epidemic outbreak of Mpox have demonstrated that viruses, despite their apparently simple structure, are sophisticated microorganisms that have evolved complicated pro-survival mechanisms. Their potential to manipulate cell death pathways can affect and determine the outcome of the infection cycle and the host's immune response. RNA viruses typically display a more acute and aggressive nature, as they often promote cell death. In this way, they proliferate and release their virions to infect adjacent cells and perpetuate their life cycle. Common consequences of RNA virus infection include hyperinflammatory responses in hosts, typically leading in damage to the epithelial barrier. Conversely, DNA viruses modulate these pathways to sustain a balance between the lytic cycle, during which they replicate, and latency, wherein they remain inactive until an appropriate stimulus triggers reactivation. Achieving this balance and transitioning between stages of infection requires the inhibition of cellular death processes. In both instances, the viruses seem to respond to the cellular context, enhancing their adaptability through mutations, so to deceive host defenses and therefore secure their survival. This highlights the necessity to comprehend the processes via which these biological threats induce cell death, thereby facilitating the development of broad-spectrum or targeted antiviral treatments.

articles.title: Impact of inoculum effect on in vitro activity of intermittent and continuous piperacillin-tazobactam infusion against ESBL-producing Escherichia coli in a hollow-fiber infection model.
articles.abstract:
UNLABELLED: Use of piperacillin-tazobactam (TZP) in the treatment of severe extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Escherichia coli (ESBL-EC) infections is controversial. Two features may explain treatment failures: the inoculum effect and suboptimal pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) target attainment, particularly in critically ill patients. To study the combined impact of the inoculum effect and a PK/PD optimization on the in vitro efficacy of TZP against ESBL-EC infections. Five-day hollow-fiber infection model simulating TZP pharmacokinetics in critically ill patients was performed: two TZP infusion regimens (4/0.5 g q6h over 30 min, and 16/2 g q24h continuous infusion), three ESBL-EC clinical strains: 1146 (blaCTX-M-15, MIC = 2 mg/L), 3383 (blaCTX-M-15 + blaTEM-1, MIC = 4 mg/L), and 2262 (blaCTX-M-15 + blaOXA-1, MIC = 8 mg/L), and two initial inocula (5 and 7 log10 CFU/mL). Intermittent infusion was associated with systematic bacterial regrowth within 24 h, consistent with failure to reach the 100%fT >4× MIC threshold. Continuous infusion resulted in undetectable bacterial count for the strains 3383 (MIC = 4 mg/L, low inoculum) and 1146 (MIC = 2 mg/L, low and high inocula). For strain 3383, the inoculum effect was demonstrated by total bacterial killing in continuous infusion with low inoculum, whereas early regrowth (>10 log10 CFU/mL) with resistance emergence (MIC > 256 mg/L) was observed with high inoculum. Strain 2262 (MIC = 8 mg/L) exhibited systematic treatment failure regardless of infusion mode or inoculum size. Continuous infusion of TZP may be considered as a carbapenem-sparing agent in ESBL-EC infection with a TZP MIC ≤ 2 mg/L regardless of inoculum, or a TZP MIC of 4 mg/L at low inoculum. TZP should not be used for strains with an MIC of 8 mg/L or suspected OXA-1 co-production, irrespective of the infusion mode.

IMPORTANCE: Infections caused by extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Escherichia coli represent a growing therapeutic challenge, particularly in critically ill patients. Carbapenems remain the reference treatment, but their overuse drives resistance emergence. Piperacillin-tazobactam is a potential carbapenem-sparing agent, but its clinical efficacy remains debated, partly due to the inoculum effect (a reduction in antibiotic activity at high bacterial densities) and suboptimal dosing regimens. Using a hollow-fiber infection model simulating the pharmacokinetics of critically ill patients, this study demonstrates that continuous infusion of piperacillin-tazobactam can overcome the inoculum effect under specific conditions, defined by the MIC of the infecting strain and the estimated bacterial density. These findings support a stratified approach to piperacillin-tazobactam use in severe ESBL-producing E. coli infections, based on MIC, inoculum size, and β-lactamase profile, and may help clinicians identify patients who could safely receive piperacillin-tazobactam instead of a carbapenem.

articles.title: Cohort methods: the CANadian RADiation workers (CANRAD) cohort.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: The long-term follow-up of workers with protracted exposure to low dose occupational ionizing radiation is important to understand the health effects and risks of radiation. This paper describes the creation and record linkage of the CANadian RADiation workers (CANRAD) cohort, including the work to resolve data issues and linkage challenges to outcome databases.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: The CANRAD cohort includes all workers with occupational exposure to ionizing radiation (1951-2018) in Canada's National Dose Registry (NDR) and three facility-based sub-cohorts: Eldorado uranium workers (1932-1980), Ontario uranium miners (1954-1996), and Atomic Energy of Canada Limited nuclear workers (1956-1985). The sub-cohorts were added to the NDR to update workers' employment histories and radiation exposures to 2018. Deterministic and probabilistic record linkage methods linked the CANRAD cohort to national population-based mortality (1950-2020), cancer incidence (1969-2019), and tax (1981-2020) data.

RESULTS: Of 957,580 CANRAD workers, 883,150 (92.2%) successfully linked to Statistics Canada vital statistics databases. The analytical cohort includes 860,650 (89.9%) workers, including 427,920 (49.7%) females. At the end of follow-up, 751,520 (87.3%) of the cohort were alive and 94,410 (11.0%) were dead. Neoplasms and circulatory disease represented 63.8% (57,030) of all known causes of death (89,330). Prostate, breast, lung & bronchus, and colorectal cancer represented 49.9% (40,780) of first primary cancers (81,670). The mean cumulative effective dose was 17.1 mSv; but most cumulative doses were <10 mSv (∼85.0% of males and 98.1% of females). Females (350,510, 82.4%) dominated the medical sector.

CONCLUSIONS: The CANRAD cohort is a large and valuable cohort of Canadian occupationally exposed radiation workers with employment histories, radiation exposures and long-term follow-up of tax, mortality, and cancer incidence. Analysis of this cohort will support the radiation protection framework.

articles.title: Metaproteomic analysis of human sonicate fluid highlights neutrophil extracellular trap formation associated with periprosthetic joint infection.
articles.abstract:
UNLABELLED: Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) is a devastating complication of total joint arthroplasty that can be challenging to diagnose and treat. Neutrophils are a prominent feature in PJI, with neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) known to be present; little is known, however, about the physiology of PJI-associated NETs. Here, the proteomes of PJI and non-infectious arthroplasty failure (NIAF), analyzed using liquid chromatography tandem mass-spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) and proximity extension assay (PEA)-based profiling of fluids derived from sonication of arthroplasty components removed from patients who had undergone revision arthroplasty, were compared, with a focus on NET formation. In addition, in vitro effects of synovial fluid components on Staphylococcus aureus-induced NET formation were characterized. LC-MS/MS (PJI n = 85, NIAF n = 26) and PEA (PJI n = 95, NIAF n = 39) showed NET formation and neutrophil degranulation to be associated with PJI, with the complement cascade and platelet activation pathways identified as potential contributors. In vitro studies showed delayed NET formation in artificial synovial fluid compared to standard cell culture media conventionally used to evaluate NETs. Together, these results demonstrate the presence of NETs in PJI, identify potential pathways involved in PJI-associated NETosis, and point to an influence of synovial components on NET formation during PJI.

IMPORTANCE: Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) is a major complication of joint replacement, placing a significant burden on patients and the healthcare system. Our research reveals that neutrophils and their antimicrobial "traps" are dominant features of the immune response at the infection joint site. Importantly, we found that the unique environment of the joint delays the formation of these traps, potentially contributing to the pathogenesis of PJI. By establishing a new experimental platform tailored for the infected joint, this work provides a foundational platform for probing these mechanisms and supports the development of improved diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.

articles.title: Avian influenza A virus polymerase gene leads to temperature-resistant genome replication.
articles.abstract: Influenza A viruses (IAV) pose a persistent pandemic threat. Successful cross-species transmission from waterfowl to mammals requires host adaptation for efficient replication and spread. Avian IAVs are adapted to the temperature of the avian gut, approximately 41°C, while human IAVs replicate at 33°C in the upper respiratory tract. PB1, the catalytic core of the viral heterotrimeric RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), is essential for viral RNA synthesis. Three pandemic IAV strains (1918, 1957, and 1968) carried an avian-origin PB1 gene, suggesting a selective advantage. Fever, a critical antiviral response, elevates body temperature to 38°C or higher and can restrict viral replication. We hypothesized that avian PB1 may allow IAV replication at febrile temperatures. Using a mini-replicon system, we demonstrate that a polymerase of a seasonal human H1N1 IAV fails to replicate viral RNA efficiently at 40°C, whereas substitution of the PB1 with that from the 1918, 1957, and 1968 pandemic viruses, or a low-pathogenic avian H2N1 virus, restores RNA synthesis. Chimeric seasonal human H1N1 viruses expressing avian or 1918 PB1 replicate at 40°C in MDCK cells, unlike wild-type H1N1. Activity assays with purified chimeric IAV polymerases further suggest that avian-origin PB1 may intrinsically enhance polymerase activity at elevated temperatures. Together, these data show that avian-origin PB1 enables IAV replication at febrile temperatures, highlighting its role in zoonotic emergence and host adaptation. Surveillance of avian-origin PB1 genes in IAVs circulating in mammals may help identify strains with pandemic potential and inform the development of countermeasures.IMPORTANCEInfluenza A viruses of avian origin remain a persistent threat to human health. The 1918, 1957, and 1968 pandemic influenza viruses each acquired an avian-origin PB1 gene, but the adaptive advantage conferred by these genes remains incompletely understood. Here, we show that avian-origin PB1 genes enhance viral RNA replication by a seasonal human influenza virus polymerase at elevated temperature and enable replication of a human influenza virus at 40°C, a temperature relevant to both avian hosts and human febrile illness. PB1-dependent effects were observed in cell-based polymerase assays, with purified polymerase, and during authentic virus infection. These findings identify temperature-resistant genome replication as a potential adaptive property of avian-origin PB1 and suggest that acquisition of an avian PB1 may help influenza viruses overcome temperature barriers encountered during adaptation to mammalian hosts.

articles.journal: Journal of magnetic resonance imaging : JMRI

articles.title: Evaluation of Otolaryngology Residency and Faculty Demographics Following the Single Accreditation System.
articles.journal: Otolaryngology--head and neck surgery : official journal of American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery (OHNS) residency remains highly competitive, with persistent disparities in applicant representation. This study presents a cross-sectional analysis of OHNS residency and faculty demographics using 2025 program rosters, evaluating degree type (MD vs DO), geographic distribution, and leadership influence.

STUDY DESIGN: A cross-sectional review.

SETTING: All US ACGME-accredited OHNS residency programs, with data collected in 2024 to 2025.

METHODS: Demographic data were collected on OHNS faculty and residents, including post-graduate year (PGY) 1 through PGY5 trainees at the time of data collection, corresponding to entry years from 2020 to 2024 across all US ACGME-accredited residency programs. Data was extracted from official program websites, FREIDA, ACGME, NRMP, and social media. Programs with incomplete data, those using the military match, and non-accredited sites were excluded. Descriptive statistics, χ2 tests, and correlation analyses were performed (p < .05).

RESULTS: Of 131 programs, 125 were analyzed at the program level and 121 at the faculty level. DO residents were concentrated in Michigan (59%), Ohio (50%), and Oklahoma (50%). DO representation correlated with DO faculty (r = .82, p < .0001), DO program director (r = .95, p < .0001), and former AOA program designation (r = .92, p < .0001). A negative correlation existed between program size and DO resident (r = -.4, p < .0001).

CONCLUSION: Despite growing diversity following the single accreditation system, disparities persist in OHNS. DO residents remain underrepresented and geographically concentrated, with representation strongly associated with osteopathic faculty presence, program leadership, and prior AOA affiliation.

articles.title: The Outcomes of Slide Tracheoplasty for Complete Tracheal Rings in Children With a Tracheal Bronchus.
articles.journal: Otolaryngology--head and neck surgery : official journal of American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To compare airway presentation and outcomes following slide tracheoplasty for congenital tracheal stenosis with complete tracheal rings in children with and without a tracheal bronchus.

STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study.

SETTING: Quaternary pediatric referral center.

METHODS: Children undergoing slide tracheoplasty for complete tracheal rings between 2001 and 2021 were included. Clinical variables and outcomes were compared by tracheal bronchus status. Propensity score matching was performed to adjust for baseline differences. Operative success was defined as a symptom-free, non-tracheostomy-dependent airway.

RESULTS: Among 160 children, 64 (40.0%) had a tracheal bronchus. Children without a tracheal bronchus presented at a younger age (median 184 vs 432 days; P = .014) and more frequently had stenosis involving >80% of the trachea (40.6% vs 12.5%; P = .0005) and bronchial extension (28.1% vs 12.5%; P = .032). Preoperatively, children without a tracheal bronchus were more often mechanically ventilated (49.0% vs 29.7%; P = .023) and had higher rates of cardiopulmonary arrest (15.6% vs 1.56%; P = .008). Postoperatively, they experienced longer ventilation (median, 41.5 vs 24 hours; P = .030), longer intensive care unit stay (13.5 vs 6 days; P = .005), and higher rates of bronchial stenosis (34.4% vs 14.1%; P = .0074). Operative success was higher in the tracheal bronchus group (92.2% vs 78.1%; P = .035). After propensity matching, no differences were observed in operative success (82.0% vs 90.0%; P = .815).

CONCLUSION: A tracheal bronchus was associated with a less severe airway presentation. Modification of the slide tracheoplasty technique to accommodate the aberrant bronchus does not have inferior outcomes.

articles.title: Impact of clinical frailty on mortality after elective surgery in patients aged ≥ 90 years admitted to critical care: a  binational intensive care registry analysis.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Increasing numbers of patients aged ≥ 90 years require elective surgery. Frailty is increasingly recognised as a key determinant of peri-operative risk, but high-quality evidence to understand the impact on outcomes in this age group is limited.

METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society Adult Patient Database. Patients aged ≥ 90 years admitted to ICU following elective surgery were included, encompassing planned and unplanned ICU admissions. Frailty was assessed at ICU admission using the Clinical Frailty Scale and patients categorised as non-frail or frail. Propensity score matching was performed to balance age; sex; acute illness severity; and comorbidities. Primary outcome was 1-year all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included ICU mortality; in-hospital mortality; return to pre-admission residence; and ICU and duration of hospital stay.

RESULTS: The matched cohort comprised 5398 patients (2699 without frailty (Clinical Frailty Scale 1-4) and 2699 living with frailty (Clinical Frailty Scale 5-8)), with good post-matching covariate balance. Mortality in ICU was low and not significantly different between patients who were frail and non-frail. Frailty was independently associated with higher in-hospital mortality (matched hazard ratio (HR) 1.66, 95%CI 1.22-2.27, p = 0.001) and higher 1-year mortality (matched HR 1.66, 95%CI 1.47-1.87, p < 0.001). Patients without frailty had higher odds of returning to their pre-admission residence at hospital discharge than patients living with frailty (matched OR 1.45, 95%CI 1.29-1.62, p < 0.001). Patients who were frail experienced longer hospital stays and higher rates of postoperative complications, including delirium and acute renal failure.

DISCUSSION: Among patients aged ≥ 90 years undergoing elective surgery with postoperative intensive care admission, frailty is strongly associated with prolonged recovery and worse short and long-term outcomes. Incorporation of frailty assessment into peri-operative pathways may improve risk stratification, shared decision-making and personalised care for patients aged ≥ 90 years.

articles.title: Direct oral anticoagulants vs dual antiplatelet therapy after left atrial appendage occlusion: a meta-analysis of trials.
Fructose metabolic heterogeneity drives vancomycin tolerance in clonal Staphylococcus aureus biofilms.
articles.abstract: Bacterial biofilms are characterized by profound heterogeneity, which is a primary driver of their antibiotic recalcitrance and a major obstacle to clinical infection control. However, how metabolic heterogeneity underpins collective antibiotic tolerance within biofilms remains poorly understood, particularly at single-cell resolution. Here, we apply single-cell RNA sequencing to dissect the response of Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 12600 biofilms to vancomycin. We show that vancomycin induces heterogeneous upregulation of the fructose metabolism genes fruA and fruK, which spatially segregates the biofilm into metabolically active and metabolically reduced subpopulations. Active cells exhibit increased fructose consumption, which fuels peptidoglycan biosynthesis and promotes cell wall thickening, as a mechanism that directly enhances vancomycin tolerance. In contrast, certain metabolically reduced subpopulations potentiate oxidative stress repair programs, representing an alternative survival strategy. In a diabetic mouse model characterized by impaired fructose clearance, elevated systemic fructose levels exacerbate pulmonary S. aureus infection, indicating that fructose utilization may reflect clinically relevant features of host susceptibility. Together, our findings uncover a fundamental link between metabolic heterogeneity and antibiotic tolerance in S. aureus biofilms, opening new avenues for the rational design of anti-biofilm therapeutics.

articles.title: Associations of base excess and alactic base excess with KDIGO stage 2 - 3 acute kidney injury in patients with acute ischemic stroke.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: To identify the associations of base excess (BE) and alactic base excess (aBE) with KDIGO stage 2 - 3 acute kidney injury (AKI) in patients with acute ischemic stroke (AIS).

MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this cohort study, 1,377 adult patients with AIS were identified from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) database. A univariable logistic regression model was used to explore the associations of all variables with KDIGO stage 2 - 3 AKI during the ICU stay of patients. Confounding factors were screened using bidirectional stepwise regression. Subgroup analysis was stratified based on age, Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA), and comorbidities. Forest plot was plotted to identify the associations of BE and aBE with KDIGO stage 2 - 3 AKI in AIS patients in different subgroups. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) was plotted.

RESULTS: A total of 1,377 participants were included, of whom 680 developed KDIGO stage 2 - 3 AKI during their ICU stay. After adjusting for covariates including SOFA, sodium, anticoagulants, furosemide, and aspirin, we found that the association between BE < -5.124 mmol/L and KDIGO stage 2 - 3 AKI was significant (OR = 1.51, 95% CI: 1.05 - 2.16). As for aBE, we observed that aBE < -3.444 mmol/L might be related to KDIGO stage 2 - 3 AKI (OR = 1.57, 95% CI: 1.12 - 2.20). In the adjusted model, aBE < -3.444 mmol/L was associated with elevated OR of KDIGO stage 2 - 3 AKI in AIS patients (OR = 1.43, 95% CI: 1.00 - 2.04). RCS revealed the non-liner associations of BE and aBE with KDIGO stage 2 - 3 AKI in AIS patients.

CONCLUSION: Low BE or aBE were associated with an increased risk of KDIGO stage 2 - 3 AKI in patients with AIS.

articles.title: Association of IL-8 rs4073 -251T>A gene polymorphism with diabetic nephropathy in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Diabetic nephropathy (DN) is one of the most common microvascular complications of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and a leading cause of chronic kidney disease worldwide. Inflammatory pathways play a key role in the pathogenesis and progression of DN. Interleukin-8 (IL-8), a pro-inflammatory cytokine involved in leukocyte recruitment and activation, has been associated with renal inflammation and albuminuria. However, the contribution of IL-8 gene polymorphisms to susceptibility and progression of DN remains unclear.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: This cross-sectional case-control study included 138 patients with T2DM and 138 age- and sex-matched healthy controls. Diabetic patients were stratified according to the presence of DN based on urinary albumin excretion and diabetic retinopathy. Genomic DNA was isolated from peripheral blood samples, and the IL-8 rs4073 -251T>A polymorphism was determined using polymerase chain reaction-restriction fragment length polymorphism (PCR-RFLP) analysis. Genotype and allele frequencies were compared between groups, and clinical and laboratory parameters were evaluated according to genotype status.

RESULTS: Genotype distributions of the IL-8 rs4073 -251T>A polymorphism were similar between T2DM patients and controls, suggesting no association with the development of T2DM. Among diabetic patients, however, the AA genotype was detected only in individuals without nephropathy and was absent in both latent and overt DN groups. Patients lacking the AA genotype demonstrated higher urinary albumin excretion and a greater frequency of nephropathy progression. DN patients also exhibited longer diabetes duration, poorer glycemic control, impaired renal function, and elevated inflammatory markers compared with patients without nephropathy. Additionally, an inverse relationship between the presence of the A allele and leukocyte and neutrophil counts was observed.

CONCLUSION: The IL-8 rs4073 -251T>A polymorphism does not appear to influence susceptibility to T2DM; however, the presence of the A allele may exert a protective effect against the development of diabetic nephropathy. This protective effect may be mediated through modulation of inflammatory pathways, as suggested by the inverse association between the A allele and inflammatory cell counts. Larger multicenter studies are required to confirm these findings.

articles.title: Recovery from liraglutide-induced acute liver injury assessed for causality using the updated RUCAM as global gold standard: A case report and literature review.
articles.journal: International journal of clinical pharmacology and therapeutics
articles.abstract: Liraglutide is a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) widely used for managing type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and obesity. Reports of liraglutide-associated hepatotoxicity are exceedingly rare. To our knowledge, this is the 9th case of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) caused by liraglutide to be reported. We present a case of a 40-year-old Chinese woman who developed acute liver injury with elevated liver enzymes following 2 weeks of liraglutide treatment for T2DM. Causality was assessed using the updated RUCAM scale, yielding a score of 7, indicating probable DILI, and the diagnosis was further confirmed by liver biopsy. Liver enzyme levels normalized after discontinuing the drug and administering liver-protective treatment within 3 weeks. Furthermore, this case report includes a comprehensive review of all published cases of liraglutide-associated DILI, emphasizing the necessity of regular hepatic-biochemistry monitoring in patients receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists such as liraglutide and providing meaningful evidence regarding their hepatotoxic risk.

articles.title: A rare case of ultrastructurally proven toxoplasmic myositis masquerading as necrotizing myopathy with emphasis on pathobiology.
articles.abstract: Toxoplasmosis is a zoonotic infection caused by the obligate protozoan Toxoplasma gondii. In an immunocompetent human host, the parasite forms bradyzoites (tissue cysts), mainly in skeletal muscle, eye, brain, or cardiac muscle, and remains latent. Once cysts are established, type 1 cytokine-based immunity controls the conversion to tachyzoites from bradyzoites. We propose that short-term immunosuppression can only cause a transient defect in this cycle of conversion control. The temporary lapse in conversion control releases few tachyzoites, and the host immunity in response gives rise to cytokines that can cause polymyositis. Myositis and the presence of a parasite in the muscle biopsy are very rare, even in immunosuppressed patients. We present a case of a young man with quadriplegia after immunosuppression for dengue-associated hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. We report a rare case of toxoplasmic myositis in a patient masquerading as necrotizing myopathy, with emphasis on the possible pathomechanism of myositis and ultrastructure of toxoplasma. We recommend that toxoplasma myositis should be included among the differentials of sudden muscular weakness, especially in an immunocompromised host. Our case highlights the crucial role of muscle biopsy in the diagnosis of toxoplasmic myositis. For early diagnosis, a systematic search for toxoplasmosis should be formulated in case of polymyositis, especially in immunocompromised patients, as a quicker identification of the parasite is possible and treatment response is also better in the early, acute phase of toxoplasmic myositis.

articles.title: Investigating Mediating Factors in the Genetic Link Between Maternal Smoking Around Birth and Offspring's Cardiovascular Disease Risk.
articles.journal: Nicotine & tobacco research : official journal of the Society for Research on Nicotine and Tobacco
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Maternal smoking around birth (MSAB) has been associated with adverse offspring health outcomes, but whether it causally increases offspring cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk remains unclear. We evaluated genetic associations of an MSAB proxy on offspring CVDs and explored potential mediating pathways.

METHODS: We conducted a two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) study using large genome-wide association study datasets predominantly of European ancestry. Genetic instruments for MSAB were obtained from offspring genotypes associated with reported maternal smoking around birth in the UK Biobank. Outcomes included atrial fibrillation (AF), heart failure (HF), coronary artery disease (CAD), and myocardial infarction (MI). Multivariable MR adjusted for offspring smoking initiation, and two-step MR mediation analyses assessed body mass index (BMI), type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), and lipid traits as potential mediators. The inverse-variance weighted method was the primary analysis.

RESULTS: Genetically predicted MSAB was associated with higher risks of AF (OR=2.23, 95% CI=1.28-3.92, p=4.93×10-3), HF (OR=3.84, 95% CI=1.91-7.76, p=1.70×10-4), and CAD (OR=4.50, 95% CI=1.16-17.51, p=0.03), but not MI. After adjustment for offspring smoking, the associations remained significant for HF (OR=3.88, 95% CI=1.57-9.55, p=3.22×10-3) and CAD (OR=6.23, 95% CI=2.23-17.40, p=4.82×10-4). Mediation analyses suggested that higher BMI and triglycerides, lower HDL-C and ApoA-I, and greater T2DM liability may partly mediate these associations.

CONCLUSIONS: Genetically proxied MSAB was associated with offspring CVD risk, particularly HF and CAD. Adiposity, dyslipidemia, and T2DM may represent important mediating pathways.

articles.title: Innate immune signaling relays environmental cues to mitophagy for metabolic adaptation to obesity.
articles.abstract: The mechanisms by which pancreatic β cells sense and communicate environmental cues to mitochondria to maintain insulin secretion remain poorly understood. We identified that β cells transduce metabolic stress, such as during obesity or glucolipotoxicity, through the innate immune signaling adaptor TRAF6 to regulate mitochondrial quality control. TRAF6 was dispensable for β-cell function at baseline yet was essential for glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in mouse or human β cells following nutrient excess. TRAF6 was required for the recruitment of components of both ubiquitin- and receptor-mediated mitophagy pathways to clear dysfunctional mitochondria following metabolic stress. Interestingly, concomitant loss of the ubiquitin-mediated mitophagy effector Parkin restored glucose homeostasis and mitophagy flux in TRAF6-deficient β cells by relieving impediments in receptor-mediated mitophagy. Together, we found that TRAF6 forms a molecular relay linking environmental signals to multiple mitophagy pathways to equip β cells with the means to adapt to metabolic demand and prevent diabetes.Abbreviations: ADP: adenosine diphosphate; ATP: adenosine triphosphate; BNIP3: BCL2 interacting protein 3; GSIS: glucose-stimulated insulin secretion; HFD: high-fat diet; MFN2: mitofusin 2; PRKN: parkin RBR E3 ubiquitin protein ligase; RNF41/NRDP1: ring finger protein 41; SQSTM1/p62: sequestosome 1; T2D: type 2 diabetes; TAX1BP1: Tax1 binding protein 1; TLR: Toll-like receptor; TRAF6: TNF receptor associated factor 6.

articles.title: Development of a Magnetic Bead-Based Electrochemical Immunoassay for Human Immunodeficiency Virus Type 1 p24 Antigen Detection.
articles.abstract: Early and sensitive detection of human immunodeficiency virus 1 (HIV-1) p24 antigen is crucial for identifying acute infection before seroconversion and monitoring low-level viremia. Here, we report a magnetic bead (MB)-based electrochemical immunoassay using stencil-printed carbon electrodes, systematically comparing streptavidin-, tosyl-, and N-hydroxysuccinimide-MBs for p24 detection. Tosyl-MBs achieved superior analytical performance with limits of detection of 19.4 pg/mL in tris-buffered saline with Tween 20, 24.3 pg/mL in media containing viral lysis buffer, and 8.8 pg/mL in human serum, demonstrating excellent matrix tolerance and reproducibility across the clinically relevant concentration range. The sandwich immunoassay employed optimized capture and horseradish peroxidase-conjugated detection antibodies with chronoamperometric readout using 3,3',5,5'-tetramethylbenzidine substrate at 0.0 V vs a silver pseudoreference electrode, enabling rapid immunocomplex quantification on magnet-retained beads with minimal sample handling. Tosyl-MBs provided the strongest concentration-dependent response across all matrices tested, with surface chemistry influencing antibody immobilization efficiency, nonspecific background signal, and p24 capture capacity. The platform demonstrated stability for at least 28 days under storage conditions and successfully distinguished inactivated HIV-1 samples from negative controls, thereby establishing tosyl-MB electrochemical immunoassays that are compatible with serum and other complex biological matrices. Further validation with clinical specimens, integration of simplified sample-processing steps, and implementation in portable instrumentation will be required to assess their potential for future point-of-care HIV diagnostics.

articles.title: Modeling finishing pig growth performance and carcass response to dietary net energy using ingredient nutrient values from four different databases.
articles.abstract: Data from 91 grow-finish pig experiments with diets differing in net energy (NE) and other nutrients were used in a meta-analysis to model growth performance and carcass characteristics based on the diet's NE, crude protein (CP), standardized ileal digestible (SID) Lys, neutral detergent fiber (NDF), and lysine to NE (Lys:NE) ratio. Energy and nutrient concentrations in all diets were determined using values from four different databases (NRC, 2012 [NRC]; CVB, 2022 [CVB]; INRA, 2024 [INRA]; Rostagno et al., 2024 [BR]). Stepwise selection using Akaike information criteria was used for model selection considering the linear, quadratic, and interactive effects of NE, SID Lys, CP, NDF, Lys:NE ratio, and body weight. Model variable predictors were generated using a linear mixed model. Selected models indicated that ADG and G:F increased as dietary NE increases in the four databases evaluated. However, the magnitude of response in G:F differed between ingredient databases at the early and late stages of the finishing period. The model using BR database appears to overestimate ADG when diets with concentrations of NDF are used. The 4 models predicted greater changes in ADG and G:F when the Lys:NE ratio was maintained compared to when a constant SID Lys level was used. Dressing percentage (DP), backfat depth (BF), and loin depth (LD) increased and percentage lean (PL) decreased as NE increased with different magnitudes of response depending on the database. However, when a constant Lys:NE ratio was not maintained, increasing NE did not change DP predictions using the BR database, with the NRC and INRA models predicting a slight increase only at high NE levels. The CVB model suggested a similar response in DP whether Lys:NE ratio was maintained or not. For all the ingredient databases, BF and PL were predicted to linearly increase and decrease, respectively, as NE increased whether the Lys:NE ratio was maintained or not, but the changes were greater without maintaining the Lys:NE ratio. The models predicted LD to increase quadratically, with a greater response at low NE levels and the response plateauing at high dietary NE, regardless of whether the Lys to NE was maintained or not. In conclusion, the models generated provide estimates of the magnitude of the change for growth and carcass parameters of grow-finish pigs when dietary NE and other nutrients changed, with the magnitude of the changes being greater when Lys:NE ratio are maintained compared to constant levels of Lys.

articles.title: Inverse probability weighting-based mediation analysis for microbiome data.
articles.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Mediation analysis is an important tool for elucidating causal mechanisms in biomedical research and has recently gained increasing attention in microbiome studies. Motivated by a microbiome study of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients, we investigate whether the effect of induction chemotherapy intensity on infection status is mediated through gut microbial taxa. This problem poses substantial methodological challenges due to the high dimensionality, zero inflation, and dependence of microbial mediators, as well as the presence of an exposure-induced mediator-outcome confounder, antibiotic use.

RESULTS: To address these challenges, we propose a novel nonparametric identification formula for the interventional indirect effect, a causal mediation estimand that remains identifiable in the presence of exposure-induced mediator-outcome confounding. Building on this identification result, we develop an inverse probability weighting estimator and construct standard normal bootstrap confidence intervals for inference. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed method achieves accurate effect estimation and maintains appropriate type I error rates and power in finite samples. Application to the AML microbiome study provides evidence of a statistically significant interventional indirect effect of induction chemotherapy intensity on infection risk through alterations in the gut microbiome.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: The R code for the simulation studies is available at https://github.com/YX-ZHANG-1/CausalMediationMicrobiome and archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21960802.

articles.title: Surface charge alterations in urinary extracellular vesicles mirror diabetic kidney disease pathophysiology.
articles.abstract: Urinary extracellular vesicles (uEVs) are an attractive source of biomarkers as their cargo of proteins, nucleic acids and lipids reflects cell pathophysiology. The physical properties of uEVs such as their electrical nature measured by the zeta potential (charge at the interface of vesicle and liquid) are seldom explored although their understanding may lead to translational applications of EVs in clinical settings. In diabetes and diabetic kidney disease (DKD), post-translational modifications resulting from loss of glycocalyx (diabetes) and gain of extracellular matrix components (tissue fibrosis) could potentially affect the electrical charge of pathologically relevant EVs. DKD cohorts obtained by adhering to industry-standard reproducible criteria were stratified into stable and progressive disease based on estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) loss and compared to nonkidney disease diabetic and healthy controls. Surface charge analysis revealed a significant difference in the zeta potential of large uEVs between the diabetic and healthy cohorts, as well as between the diabetic and DKD-progressive cohorts. These differences are mechanistically consistent with pathological alterations observed in heparan sulfate (HS) content. Accordingly, uEVs from DKD patients exhibited higher HS levels than those from diabetic individuals, as assessed by SP-IRIS/ExoView using HS-binding capture. Comparative proteomic analysis further demonstrated an increased abundance of the sulfated glycosaminoglycan lumican in DKD uEVs relative to diabetes, consistent with its reported upregulation in early fibrotic stages of DKD. Notably, our findings indicate for the first time that the zeta potential of large uEVs may be predictive of the progression of diabetes into DKD.

articles.title: Gestational heat stress alters maternal vaginal microbiome, plasma metabolic markers, and preweaning offspring performance in Bos indicus-influenced cow-calf pairs.
articles.abstract: This 3-year study evaluated the effects of gestational access to shade on maternal performance, vaginal microbiome composition, and offspring preweaning performance in beef cows. On day 0 of each year (92 ± 20 days prepartum), 176 multiparous, pregnant Brangus crossbred beef cows (25 to 37.5% Bos indicus) were stratified by bull, body weight (BW; 548 ± 51 kg) and body condition score (BCS; 5.52 ± 0.70; scale of 1 to 9), and randomly assigned to 1 of 16 bahiagrass (Paspalum notatum) pastures (11 cows and 8.1 ha per pasture). Treatments were randomly assigned to pastures on day 0 of each year (8 pastures per treatment) and consisted of cows provided (SH) or not (NSH) access to artificial shade (3.27 m2 per cow) from day 0 to 90. Cows were provided free-choice access to artificial shade from day 91 until calf weaning on day 330 (240 ± 20 days of age). Non-binary and binary data were analyzed as a complete randomized study using the MIXED and GLIMMIX procedure of SAS, respectively. Effects of treatment × day × year and treatment × year were not detected (P ≥ 0.11) for any variable, except for calf preweaning BW (P = 0.01). Shade access improved (P ≤ 0.05) cow BCS on days 30, 60, and 150 and modified plasma metabolites, including lower cortisol on day 30 and greater glucose and IGF-1 but lower urea nitrogen on day 60. Shade also reduced (P ≤ 0.05) body surface and rectal temperatures on day 60, respiration rates, and intravaginal temperatures from 1000 to 1400 h. Plasma non-esterified fatty acids, whole blood mRNA expression of heat shock proteins, and reproductive success did not differ (P ≥ 0.12) between treatments. Relative abundance of Blautia and Methanobrevibacter on day 30 were greater (P ≤ 0.05) in SH vs. NSH cows. At birth, gestational access to shade did not impact (P ≥ 0.41) calf plasma cortisol and serum immunoglobulin G but increased (P ≤ 0.05) calf plasma haptoglobin and BW. At weaning, calf BW was greater (P ≤ 0.04) in year 1 but was less (P = 0.05) in years 2 and 3 for NSH vs. SH calves. In conclusion, gestational shade access improved maternal thermoregulation, body condition, and metabolic profile, while modestly shifting the prepartum vaginal microbiome. These maternal responses were accompanied by greater calf birth weight, although weaning performance varied by year, underscoring the dynamic nature of gestational heat stress impacts in subtropical grazing systems.

articles.title: Current and emerging neuromodulation techniques for motor recovery after ischemic stroke: a 2026 update.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Neuromodulation technologies have emerged as promising tools to enhance motor recovery following ischemic stroke. Acute reperfusion therapy remains highly time-dependent, underscoring the need for interventions that augment post-stroke neuroplasticity. Brain stimulation techniques aim to modulate cortical excitability and promote adaptive reorganization of motor networks during the critical recovery period after stroke.

AREAS COVERED: The authors review recent advances in neuromodulation strategies for post-stroke motor recovery, as well as the key principles underlying neuromodulation. Major noninvasive modalities, including transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), and low-intensity focused ultrasound stimulation (LIFUS), are reviewed alongside emerging applications of invasive techniques such as deep brain stimulation (DBS) and vagus nerve stimulation (VNS). Recent randomized clinical trials and translational studies are also highlighted. This article is based on literature obtained through PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov searches for content published between 1 January 2020 and 30 March 202630 March 2026 and was supplemented by earlier landmark studies relevant to stroke recovery and neuromodulation.

EXPERT OPINION: Although neuromodulation technologies demonstrate encouraging safety profiles, clinical trial results feature notable neutral results. Future studies bear the burden of refining stimulation paradigms, patient selection, and rehabilitation dosing, possibly leveraging personalized, biomarker-driven patient selection.

articles.title: A review on recent advances in regenerative medicine for renal diseases: Approaches and challenges.
articles.journal: Developmental dynamics : an official publication of the American Association of Anatomists
articles.abstract: Renal diseases such as acute and chronic kidney disease cause loss of nephrons and kidney function, often leading to renal failure. Current treatments like dialysis and transplantation only manage symptoms and extend survival for a few years. Regenerative medicine offers promising approaches for repairing and regenerating renal tissue by targeting underlying disease mechanisms. For this narrative review, relevant original research articles and review articles were retrieved from online databases such as PubMed, Google Scholar, and ScienceDirect by using relevant keywords such as "renal regeneration," "kidney organoids," "stem cell therapy," "gene therapy," "extracellular vesicles," and "tissue engineering." The literature search focused primarily on articles published between 2020 and 2026 to discuss the recent advancements in regenerative approaches for renal disease. Recent advances in regenerative medicine have identified therapies such as stem cells, gene therapy, CRISPR-Cas9, extracellular vesicles, and kidney organoids that promote nephron regeneration, improve vascularization, regulate inflammation, and restore kidney function. This review highlights the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying renal damage, recent advances in regenerative medicine, and the key challenges and future directions for the safe and effective use of regenerative medicine in treating renal diseases.

articles.title: Stage-Specific Patterns of Imaging and Non-Motor Biomarkers in Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 3.
articles.journal: Annals of clinical and translational neurology
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Advancements in disease-modifying therapies for spinocerebellar ataxia Type 3 (SCA3) underscore the need for robust biomarkers to monitor disease progression and evaluate treatment efficacy. Although motor phenotypes have been well characterized, less is known about non-motor and imaging-based features across different disease stages. This study aimed to characterize stage-specific patterns of non-motor and imaging biomarkers in SCA3.

METHODS: This cross-observational study included 229 patients with SCA3 and 104 age- and sex-matched healthy controls from the Organization for Southeast China for cerebellar ataxia research. Non-motor symptoms were assessed using a battery of neuropsychological tests. Brain volume loss was assessed by 3.0-Tesla MRI with regions-of-interest (ROI)-based volumetric analysis. Neuroinflammation was quantified in vivo using translocator protein positron emission tomography (TSPO-PET) with the 18F-DPA-714 radioligand. Additive regression models were fitted to evaluate the cross-sectional associations between biomarkers and disease stages. Receiver operating curve (ROC) analyses were applied to estimate the discriminative ability of the candidate biomarkers.

RESULTS: Non-motor symptoms, including cognitive functions, anxiety, fatigue, depression, and sleep quality, declined after ataxia onset in SCA3. Volume loss in the brainstem and ventral diencephalon diverged from normal controls at 0.7 and 0.2 years before ataxia onset, respectively. Correspondingly, the TSPO signal in the brainstem and ventral diencephalon increased and deviated from normal throughout the disease course.

INTERPRETATION: Our findings propose a staging model of SCA3 that includes a biomarker stage characterized by multidimensional objective indicators of neurodegeneration and neuroinflammation from pre-ataxia to ataxia onset.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04010214.

articles.title: Six-month supervised telerehabilitation combining pilates-based therapeutic exercise and self-myofascial release in adults with fibromyalgia: a randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effects of a 6-month supervised multicomponent telerehabilitation programme combining Pilates-based therapeutic exercise and self-myofascial release on fibromyalgia impact, sleep quality, and psychological outcomes.

DESIGN: Two-arm, parallel-group randomized controlled trial.

SUBJECTS/PATIENTS: 68 adults with fibromyalgia confirmed according to the 2016 ACR criteria.

METHODS: Participants were randomized to a 6-month supervised home-based telerehabilitation programme (n = 35) or usual care (n = 33). The intervention comprised 3 live online sessions weekly combining Pilates-based therapeutic exercise, self-myofascial release, core stabilization, low-load resistance exercise, stretching, and relaxation. Outcomes were assessed at baseline, 3 months, and 6 months using validated patient-reported measures.

RESULTS: Significant group-by-time interactions were observed for fibromyalgia impact (p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.132), sleep quality (p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.129), depressive symptoms (p = 0.002, partial η2 = 0.129), and perceived stress (p = 0.028, partial η2 = 0.065), but not for anxiety (p = 0.701). Mean intervention adherence was 87.5%, with no adverse or serious adverse events reported in either group.

CONCLUSION: 6 months of supervised multicomponent telerehabilitation produced favourable longitudinal changes in fibromyalgia impact, sleep quality, depressive symptoms, and perceived stress compared with usual care.

articles.title: Cognitive assessment in post-stroke delirium: distinguishing impairment from instability.
The Added Value of 18F-FDG PET/CT in Children With Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis Presenting as a Clinically Isolated Lesion.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The clinical utility of 18F-FDG PET/CT in children diagnosed with Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) who present with a clinically isolated lesion remains unclear. This study aimed to assess the added value of 18F-FDG PET/CT in identifying occult lesions and assessing its impact on disease classification and clinical outcomes in this patient population.

METHODS: This retrospective study included children who underwent surgical resection of a clinically isolated lesion, were confirmed to have LCH by histopathology, and received 18F-FDG PET/CT prior to initiation of systemic therapy. Outcomes including detection of additional lesions, disease reclassification, and progression-free survival were analyzed. Kaplan-Meier analysis with log-rank test was used to compare progression-free survival between groups.

RESULTS: A total of 44 children were included (median age 4.29 years; 70.5% male). 18F-FDG PET/CT identified additional lesions in 24 patients (54.5%), leading to reclassification as single-system multifocal disease in 10 (22.7%) and multisystem disease in 14 (31.8%). Four patients (9.1%) had risk organ involvement. 18F-FDG PET/CT findings altered the treatment strategy in 54.5% of patients. All 5 relapsed patients belonged to the group with additional lesions (p = 0.044).

CONCLUSION: 18F-FDG PET/CT detected additional lesions in over half of the children diagnosed with LCH presenting as a clinically isolated lesion, resulting in disease reclassification and improved risk stratification. 18F-FDG PET/CT should be routinely performed in this clinical scenario to ensure accurate staging and appropriate treatment.

articles.title: The Use of Adhesion Barriers in Abdominopelvic Surgery: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The efficacy and safety of adhesion barriers in preventing postoperative adhesions remain uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of adhesion barriers in reducing postoperative adhesions following abdominopelvic surgery.

METHODS: CENTRAL, EMBASE and MEDLINE were searched from inception to January 15, 2025 for parallel-arm randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing adhesion barriers with controls in patients undergoing abdominopelvic surgery. Case series, case reports, reviews, animal studies, observational studies and studies involving patients with pre-existing adhesions were excluded.

RESULTS: Thirty-six RCTs involving 6729 patients were included. Adhesion barriers significantly reduced the incidence of postoperative adhesions on second-look assessment compared with controls (21 RCTs, n = 2351; OR 0.37, 95% CI 0.30-0.45, p < 0.00001; I2 = 51%; certainty of evidence: moderate). Subgroup analyses demonstrated significant reductions in postoperative adhesions in both general surgery (9 studies, n = 1162; OR 0.38, 95% CI 0.27-0.53, p < 0.00001; I2 = 27%) and obstetrics and gynecology (12 studies, n = 1189; OR 0.36, 95% CI 0.27-0.47, p < 0.00001; I2 = 62%). Pooled analysis demonstrated no significant differences between the adhesion barrier and control groups in the incidence of anastomotic leakage (9 RCTs, n = 1541), abscess formation (6 RCTs, n = 1182), wound infection (11 RCTs, n = 1084), time between initial surgery and second surgery (10 RCTs, n = 874), intraoperative blood loss (15 RCTs, n = 5327) and adhesion severity (11 RCTs, n = 756). Adhesion barriers were associated with a modest reduction in post-operative small bowel obstruction (12 RCTs, n = 4917; OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.99, p = 0.04; I2 = 38%), but were associated with a significantly longer duration of the index operation (18 RCTs, n = 5868; MD 18.66, 95% CI 11.25 to 26.06, p < 0.00001; I2 = 99%).

CONCLUSIONS: Adhesion barriers reduced adhesions at second-look assessment in a meta-analysis of pooling eight heterogeneous agent classes and procedures against an inconsistently scored surrogate outcome. Thus, evidence remains insufficient to recommend routine use or to define which patients, procedures, or risk levels warrant its use. Until adequately powered, agent-specific trials with standardized scoring and patient-centered endpoints exist, adhesion-barrier use should remain an individual clinical decision, not standard care.

PROSPERO REGISTRATION: CRD42024595564.

articles.title: Haemodiafiltration, haemofiltration and haemodialysis for adults with kidney failure.
authors: supported by Cochrane Kidney and Transplant
articles.journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
articles.abstract:
RATIONALE: Convective extracorporeal dialysis modalities, haemofiltration (HF), haemodiafiltration (HDF), and acetate-free biofiltration (AFB), remove excess body fluid across the dialysis membrane through an interplay of positive and negative pressures and accumulated middle- and larger-sized solutes more efficiently than haemodialysis (HD). This increased removal of larger solutes, combined with the use of ultrapure dialysis fluid in convective dialysis, is hypothesised to reduce the frequency and severity of symptoms during HD and improve long-term clinical outcomes. This is an update of a review first published in 2006 and updated in 2015.

OBJECTIVES: To determine the benefits and harms of convective (HF, HDF, or AFB) versus diffusive (HD) dialysis modalities, or expanded HD (HDx), in preventing all-cause and cardiovascular death, cardiovascular morbidity, fatigue, and vascular access problems in adults with kidney failure.

SEARCH METHODS: We searched the Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase and two trial registers up to 3 April 2025. Additionally, handsearching of journals and conference abstract books was performed, and the references of the included studies were reviewed.

ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing convective therapy (HF, HDF, AFB) with another convective therapy or with diffusive therapy (HD or HDx) for treating adults with kidney failure.

OUTCOMES: Critical and important outcomes included all-cause and cardiovascular death, nonfatal cardiovascular events, fatigue, problems with vascular access, hospitalisation, and health-related quality of life (HRQoL).

RISK OF BIAS: Two authors independently assessed the risk of bias using the Cochrane RoB 1 tool.

SYNTHESIS METHODS: We summarised treatment effects using the random-effects model and reported risk ratios (RR) for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences (MD) for continuous data with 95% confidence intervals (CI). We assessed the confidence of the evidence using the GRADE approach.

INCLUDED STUDIES: We identified 62 eligible studies (6897 participants). In total, 54 studies (6525 participants) compared HF, HDF or AFB with HD (both high-flux and low-flux); two studies (24 participants) compared AFB with HDF; three studies (62 participants) compared HDF with HF; and four studies (163 participants) compared HDx with HDF/HD.

SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: Convective dialysis, compared with diffusive therapy, likely reduces the risk of death (any cause) (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.80 to 0.96; I² = 0%; 15 studies, 5463 participantss; moderate-certainty evidence due to indirectness) and cardiovascular death (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.92; I² = 0%; 9 studies, 4761 participants; moderate-certainty evidence due to indirectness). Cardiovascular morbidity was likely not different between convective and diffusive dialysis (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.22; I² = 0%; 2 studies, 2074 participants; moderate-certainty evidence due to indirectness). Little to no differences were found between convective and diffusive dialysis on fatigue (MD -0.95, 95% CI -2.50 to 0.60; 1 study, 543 participants; low-certainty evidence due to imprecision), problems with vascular access (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.50; 1 study, 124 participants; low-certainty evidence due to imprecision), hospitalisation (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.37; I² = 0%; 3 studies, 600 participants; low-certainty evidence due to indirectness and imprecision), or physical quality of life (MD 0.66, 95% CI -1.08 to 2.40; 1 study, 538 participants; low-certainty evidence due to imprecision). Direct comparisons between different convective modalities were limited and underpowered to detect meaningful differences.

AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: Convective dialysis likely reduces all-cause and cardiovascular death. Effects on nonfatal cardiovascular events, fatigue, vascular access failure, and hospitalisation are inconclusive. Future RCTs should prioritise methodological rigour and could focus on unresolved questions, including the impact of convective therapies on patient-centred outcomes such as symptom burden, HRQoL, functional status, and intradialytic tolerance, as well as investigating barriers to uptake, evaluating health system readiness, assessing cost-effectiveness, and identifying strategies to promote equitable access.

FUNDING: No specific funding.

REGISTRATION: Previous versions available via DOI: 10.1002/14651858.CD006258 and DOI: 10.1002/14651858.CD006258.pub2.

articles.title: Performance of the Expanded Cardiovascular Risk Prediction Score for Rheumatoid Arthritis: An External Validation in the BRASS Registry.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cardiovascular (CV) disease occurs more frequently in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) than in the general population and is difficult to predict. The expanded risk score for RA (ERS-RA) has demonstrated good discrimination and calibration in prior studies, but additional external validation studies are needed to understand clinical utility.

METHODS: Data from a single center RA registry was integrated with electronic health records (EHR) and linked to Medicare/Medicaid administrative claims data. A less restrictive CV outcome was defined as an event identified in any of the three data sources (questionnaires/EHR/claims), and a more restrictive outcome included events in EHR and claims. External validation of the ERS-RA examined model discrimination and calibration.

RESULTS: The longitudinal RA registry has 1,332 participants aged 20-80 years without prior evidence of CVD, followed for a mean of 6.8 years. The mean age was 54 years and 84% were female. We observed 164 (12.3%) and 69 (5.2%) participants with a CV event with the less and more restrictive CV definitions, respectively. The mean ERS-RA predicted score was 7.1%, and 424 (32%) participants had a predictive score ≥7.5%. We observed c-statistics of 0.66 (95% CI 0.62-0.71; less restrictive) and 0.80 (95% CI 0.76-0.85; more restrictive). The ERS-RA also demonstrated good calibration, with better performance for the more restrictive CV event definition.

CONCLUSIONS: The ERS-RA demonstrated good discrimination and calibration for CV risk prediction in an external validation RA cohort. It also highlights the importance of using multiple sources of data to find CV events in a non-CV registry.

articles.title: Association of Retinal Age Gap with Socioeconomic Deprivation: A Cross-Sectional Analysis of a Large Diverse Urban Cohort.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Socioeconomic deprivation is a profound determinant of health, driving systemic physiological dysregulation that may accelerate biological ageing. Retinal age gap (RAG) is a validated deep-learning-derived biomarker for accelerated ageing and systemic disease risk. This study investigates the relationship between socioeconomic deprivation and RAG in two large, distinct United Kingdom cohorts.

METHODS: We performed cross-sectional analysis within the UK Biobank (UKB) (N = 38,412) and the London-based AlzEye (N = 49,681) cohorts. Socioeconomic deprivation was defined using Townsend Index for UKB and Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD) for AlzEye. RAG was generated from colour fundus photography using a pre-trained deep learning model. We applied linear regression modelling to examine associations between deprivation and RAG, sequentially adjusting for chronological age, sex, ethnicity, hypertension, and diabetes.

RESULTS: The AlzEye cohort was older, more diverse, and had more comorbidities compared to the UKB cohort. Modelled per decile of decreasing deprivation, there was significant association with decreased RAG in both UKB (-0.11 years per decile; 95% CI -0.13 to -0.10; p < 0.001) and AlzEye (-0.43 years per decile; 95% CI -0.46 to -0.39; p < 0.001). Following full adjustment, association remained significant in UKB (-0.04 years per decile; p < 0.001) but was attenuated and non-significant in AlzEye (-0.002 years per decile; p = 0.82).

CONCLUSIONS: Socioeconomic deprivation is associated with accelerated retinal ageing, although influenced by cohort characteristics and underlying health status. Signal attenuation in AlzEye suggests comorbidities may mediate impact of deprivation on retinal ageing. Longitudinal research is required to disentangle complex interplay, ensuring equitable utility of oculomic biomarkers in precision medicine.

articles.title: Interpreting the Association Between Plasma Citrulline and Bloodstream Infection in Pediatric Acute Myeloid Leukemia.
NIHSS cutoff scores for predicting FIM motor severity at discharge in acute stroke.
articles.abstract: Early estimation of activities of daily living outcomes after acute stroke is important for rehabilitation and discharge planning. The aims were to (1) examine Functional Independence Measure (FIM) motor, cognitive, and total score distributions and floor and ceiling effects at discharge; (2) determine the incremental explanatory value of the acute-phase National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS); and (3) derive and internally validate NIHSS cutoff rules for distinguishing adjacent FIM motor severity levels and evaluate their incremental classification value. This retrospective cohort included 974 patients; cognitive and total FIM analyses included 969. Regression analyses and a stratified 70:30 derivation-validation split were used. Ceiling effects were observed for the FIM motor (19.2%), cognitive (34.7%), and total scores (16.0%), whereas no floor effects were observed. Adding NIHSS to clinical variables increased the explained variance for the FIM motor (ΔR2 = 0.253), cognitive (ΔR2 = 0.332), and total scores (ΔR2 = 0.292; all p < .001). Higher NIHSS scores, older age, higher pre-stroke modified Rankin Scale scores, and hemorrhagic stroke were associated with greater FIM motor severity. The NIHSS >17 and >5 rules distinguished severe from moderate and moderate from mild severity, with validation-sample AUCs of 0.777 and 0.780. Adding these rules to baseline models improved the validation-sample AUCs for both comparisons, although paired classification accuracy improved significantly only for severe versus moderate severity. Sensitivity was below 0.70 in some analyses. NIHSS cutoff rules may provide reference points for estimating FIM motor severity at discharge but should not be used as stand-alone predictors.

articles.title: Reimagining Dental Education: Consensus Recommendations for Strengthening Faculty Pathways and Academic Career Success.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Since the beginning of the 21st century, national reports have warned that dental education is not recruiting and retaining enough oral health faculty, even as student bodies grow and become more diverse and the professions increase the emphasis on oral health's intersection with overall health. The faculty who prepare future clinicians and scientists are in short supply, and this shortage compromises the quality of dental education and ultimately impacts the quality of care delivered to our communities.

OBJECTIVE: To develop consensus recommendations to increase and sustain dental faculty for the oral health professions, addressing financial, debt, and pathway barriers to recruiting and retaining oral health faculty while strengthening research and scholarship.

CONSENSUS PROCESS: Our group (Working Group 3) consisted of eight participants, including dental school deans, clinician-educators, clinician-scientists, national and federal leaders, and a summit scholar. The group reviewed national reports, peer-reviewed literature, and program-specific evidence before and throughout three facilitated working sessions. Consensus was defined as unanimous endorsement of each recommendation following structured deliberation, with no formal objections.

RECOMMENDATIONS: The group advanced five recommendations: faculty loan-repayment programs, earlier admission pathways, a public and professional awareness campaign, deliberate recruitment through existing fellowships and federal programs, and standardized accreditation expectations for faculty development. The public awareness campaign and the faculty loan-repayment program were prioritized as near-term and intermediate priorities, respectively, with success metrics and accountability anchored in annual reporting and a first review in 2028.

CONCLUSIONS: The academic career pathway can be improved and faculty better supported. Aligning the profession's stated priorities with meaningful financial and structural incentives would strengthen faculty recruitment and retention and sustain the workforce advancing oral health education and public health.

articles.title: Genomic diversity of human-associated Mycobacterium bovis in Canada.
articles.abstract: Human infections caused by Mycobacterium bovis in Canada are not well documented. The following study analyzed M. bovis (excluding BCG) isolates identified in public health laboratories across Canadian provinces between 2000 and 2025. Whole-genome sequencing was used to catalog mutations linked to antimicrobial resistance and evaluate the genomic relatedness of isolates. The majority of samples in this study were non-respiratory (60%). Of 74 study isolates, 69 (93%) were phenotypically sensitive to first-line drugs isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol. The most frequently encountered M. bovis clusters belonged to M. tuberculosis complex lineages La 1.7 and La 1.8. Although some isolates showed phylogenetic clustering, their lack of spatial and temporal relatedness suggested sporadic cases rather than local M. bovis transmission.
