Collectively, our results reveal a transcriptional signature consistent with dietary antioxidants such as resveratrol acting as active molecular modulators of host defence, rather than simple passive antioxidants, although direct evidence of enhanced antiviral protection (e.g. reduced viral load) remains to be established. This study highlights the utility of transcriptomic approaches to link nutritional ecology with disease dynamics, offering a framework for understanding how dietary quality shapes host defence strategies and population resilience under increasing pathogen pressure.

articles.title: Association between leukocytosis and adverse clinical outcomes in thrombocytopenic patients with acute pesticide poisoning: a cross-sectional study from a referral poisoning center in Iran.
articles.journal: International journal of environmental health research
articles.abstract: This study evaluated the association between leukocytosis and adverse clinical outcomes in patients with pesticide poisoning who also had thrombocytopenia. This cross-sectional study used medical records of patients who presented between 2016 and 2021, including 241 adult patients with confirmed pesticide poisoning. We extracted demographic data, clinical signs, laboratory parameters, and outcomes. We categorized hospitalization duration as >72 hours, 24-72 hours, and <24 hours. Leukocytosis was present in 43.2% of patients (n = 104). The overall mortality rate was 25.3% (n = 61), with 49.8% requiring intensive care unit (ICU) admission (n = 120) and 44.4% requiring intubation (n = 107). Patients with elevated WBC had higher odds of prolonged hospitalization than those with normal counts: OR = 3.36, p = 0.004 for 24-72 h; and OR = 4.63, p < 0.001 for hospitalizations longer than 72 h. Leukocytosis was also strongly associated with intubation (OR = 3.50, p < 0.001) and ICU admission (OR = 3.58, p < 0.001). After adjustment, only ICU admission and leukocytosis remained significantly associated (OR = 2.20, p = 0.024). Leukocytosis may be a valuable parameter in predicting ICU admission and hospitalization duration in thrombocytopenic patients with acute pesticide poisoning. Further prospective multicenter studies are needed.

articles.title: Capture sequencing enables enhanced genome recovery of Borrelia burgdorferi in mice.
articles.abstract: The Lyme disease spirochete, Borrelia burgdorferi, maintains a low burden during vertebrate infection. This limitation has historically proven to be particularly challenging for genome-based studies of B. burgdorferi infection and spirochete presence after antibiotic treatment. Here, we used TBDCapSeq, an oligo capture-based next- generation sequencing assay, to demonstrate its utility for genome recovery of B. burgdorferi directly from C3H- and BALB/c-infected mice. Tissue fragments from the ear, heart, tarsus, and infection-site skin were collected at 3 and 6 months post-tick infection from antibiotic-treated and untreated animals. We evaluated 59 tissues from 20 untreated mice and 48 tissues from 17 doxycycline-treated mice for spirochete burden and extent of genome recovery. In the untreated mice, genome recovery from each tissue was determined by the amount of borrelial DNA present in the sequencing library and was highest in the ear and heart, followed by the skin, and lowest in the tarsus. We established that approximately 50% of the genome could be recovered with as few as 10 spirochetes per assay and >90% recovery could be achieved with only 35 spirochete genomes. In the antibiotic-treated mice, trace quantities of fragmented Borrelia DNA were still present in tissues at 3 and 6 months. However, none of the tissue samples from these mice yielded an intact B. burgdorferi genome characteristic of a viable spirochete. Combined, our findings demonstrate that capture sequencing enables genomic analyses of B. burgdorferi directly within animal hosts.IMPORTANCELyme disease, caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi, is the most common tick-borne infection in the United States. Low pathogen burden is a major limitation of B. burgdorferi studies in animal hosts and humans that has impacted a wide range of studies ranging from diagnostics, evolutionary analyses, and pathogenesis. It has also contributed to the controversies regarding B. burgdorferi persistence after antibiotic treatment. We show that a next-generation capture sequencing-based approach can readily overcome the current limitations of B. burgdorferi genomic analyses within animal hosts. We successfully recovered abundant genomic information directly from mouse tissues, and we did not find genetic evidence of intact bacteria present after antibiotic treatment. This approach can be employed to gain further insights into B. burgdorferi and provide critical genome data during animal and human infection.

articles.title: Association of chronic kidney disease with major cardiovascular outcomes following lower extremity endovascular revascularization.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) amplifies cardiovascular risk, yet its stage-specific influence on perioperative outcomes following endovascular lower extremity revascularization (LER) for peripheral artery disease (PAD) remains poorly characterized.

METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the ACS NSQIP registry (2013-2022). Adults undergoing endovascular LER for PAD were stratified by preoperative estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) via the CKD-EPI 2021 equation: G1 (≥90), G2 (60-89), G3 (30-59), G4 (15-29), and G5 (<15 mL/min/1.73 m2 or dialysis dependent). The primary outcome was 30-day major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE: myocardial infarction, stroke, or death). Multivariable logistic regression estimated adjusted odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI).

RESULTS: Among 22,424 patients (64.6% aged ≥65 years; 36.1% women), comorbidity burden increased progressively with CKD stage. Within 30 days, 556 patients (2.5%) experienced MACE. Event rates rose stepwise: 1.5% (G1), 1.6% (G2), 2.7% (G3), 4.9% (G4), and 6.0% (G5). After adjustment for age, sex, race/ethnicity, ASA class, admission status, presenting symptoms, and preoperative hematocrit, advanced CKD remained independently associated with MACE: OR 2.30 (95% CI 1.50-3.52) for G4 and OR 3.15 (95% CI 2.28-4.35) for G5 versus G1.

CONCLUSION: CKD stage provides independent prognostic information in patients undergoing endovascular LER. Advanced CKD independently predicts 30-day MACE with a dose-response relationship across stages. Preoperative eGFR should be incorporated into perioperative risk stratification protocols to guide cardiovascular optimization and surveillance planning.

articles.title: Association of quantitative sputum Candida load with respiratory dysbiosis and airway inflammation in suspected invasive pulmonary candidiasis.
articles.abstract:
UNLABELLED: The clinical significance of Candida species isolation from sputum remains ambiguous due to the colonization-infection dilemma. Integrating quantitative culture with microbiome profiling may clarify its role, yet systematic evidence is scarce. In this exploratory study (June 2023-June 2026), we enrolled 140 hospitalized patients suspected of invasive pulmonary candidiasis (IPC) and stratified them into possible IPC (n = 36), probable IPC (n = 71), and negative control (n = 33) groups based on clinical criteria. All underwent quantitative fungal culture of sputum and metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS). Patients were stratified by sputum Candida species load into low (<105 CFU/mL), high (≥105 CFU/mL), and negative control (0 CFU/mL) groups. We investigated associations between Candida species burden, respiratory microbiota, local inflammation (IL-8), and clinical outcomes. Higher Candida species load was significantly associated with prolonged hospitalization, elevated sputum IL-8, an increased microbial dysbiosis index, and depletion of key commensals (e.g., Neisseria, Prevotella, Rothia, Streptococcus, and Veillonella). Counterintuitively, it correlated negatively with several classic bacterial pathogens (such as Acinetobacter baumannii, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa). A random forest model identified a nine-species microbiome signature that effectively discriminated probable from possible IPC (AUC, 0.877; 95% CI, 0.662-0.944). In patients with suspected IPC, higher sputum Candida species load is associated with exacerbated respiratory dysbiosis and airway inflammation. Quantitative Candida species assessment combined with microbiome signatures may serve as a complementary tool for stratifying disease severity and ecological disruption, meriting further validation in larger, multicenter cohorts.

IMPORTANCE: Respiratory specimens dominate clinical fungal cultures, yet interpreting the role of Candida spp. in sputum remains a diagnostic dilemma. Here, by integrating quantitative culture with metagenomic sequencing, we show that a high sputum Candida species load is a marker of profound ecological disruption. High Candida species burden was associated with significant depletion of key commensals, an elevated dysbiosis index, and heightened local inflammation. Counterintuitively, it correlated negatively with several classic bacterial pathogens, revealing a distinct dysbiotic signature. Moreover, a microbiome-based model accurately discriminated patients with probable invasive pulmonary candidiasis. Our findings suggest that quantitative sputum Candida species load, interpreted within the context of the microbial community, may be a practical biomarker for identifying patients with significant respiratory dysbiosis and inflammation, offering a path toward more refined, ecology-informed therapeutic strategies.

articles.title: Loss of PmpC in Chlamydia trachomatis leads to altered bacterial development and impaired recovery from IFNγ- and penicillin-induced stress.
articles.abstract: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular pathogen that can reversibly halt replication and developmental transitions in response to immunological or pharmacological stress, a phenomenon linked to chlamydial persistence. Although polymorphic membrane proteins (Pmps) are known adhesins, their broader roles in other pathogenesis-relevant processes remain poorly understood. Here, we characterized a pmpC-null mutant generated by insertional mutagenesis and found that while PmpC is not essential for primary growth, it is required for the efficient transition from reticulate bodies to infectious elementary bodies during recovery from IFNγ- and penicillin-induced stress. High-resolution microscopy and temporal expression analysis revealed that PmpC localizes to the bacterial periphery throughout the developmental cycle and is released into the lumen of pathogen-containing vacuoles (inclusions), suggesting a role beyond bacterial attachment to host cells. The absence of PmpC leads to clustered bacterial distribution and reduced bacterial mobility within the inclusion. These defects correlate with delayed cellular invasion and impaired dissemination to adjacent host cells. Notably, the significance of PmpC in penicillin-induced persistence was validated using an ex vivo murine uterine horn model. Altogether, our findings reveal PmpC as a multifunctional virulence factor that mediates stress recovery, regulates bacterial distribution and dynamics within the inclusion, modulates early invasion and facilitates lateral spread, expanding its recognized role as an adhesin.IMPORTANCEChlamydia trachomatis is a leading cause of sexually transmitted infections and preventable blindness globally. A significant challenge in controlling chlamydial diseases is the ability of these bacteria to enter a reversibly non-replicating "persistent" state to survive immune pressure, nutritional stress, or antibiotic treatment. In this study, we identify the surface protein PmpC as a multifunctional factor required for bacterial recovery from IFNγ- and penicillin-induced stress, in both tissue culture and an ex vivo murine model of uterine infection. Furthermore, we found that PmpC modulates invasion and bacterial spatial distribution within the inclusion. These findings uncover novel roles for PmpC as a virulence factor in C. trachomatis infection.

articles.title: HSV-1 induces stable associations between the Golgi and endosomes within the cytoplasmic viral assembly compartment of neuronal cells.
articles.abstract: Assembly of mature herpesvirus particles is associated with extensive rearrangement of cytoplasmic membranes. Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) infection in neuronal cells induces the formation of a distinctive cytoplasmic viral assembly compartment (cVAC), in which rearranged host membranes and viral proteins are clustered at the perinuclear microtubule-organizing center (MTOC). Although both the trans-Golgi network (TGN) and endosomal compartments have been implicated as membrane sources for cytoplasmic envelopment, how secretory and endosomal pathways are reorganized and associated within the cVAC remains unclear. Here, we treated HSV-1-infected cells with nocodazole at a post-entry stage to disperse membrane components of the cVAC and identify microtubule-independent membrane organizations and associations using immunofluorescence imaging. We found that the Golgi apparatus was fragmented during infection but maintained cisternal stacking, as the Golgi markers GM130, GalT, and GRASP65 remained colocalized in both the absence and presence of nocodazole. We further demonstrated that Golgi mini-stacks retained their association with Rab6 during HSV-1 infection and formed microtubule-independent associations with early and recycling endosomes, resulting in the formation of Golgi-endosome super-mini-stacks. Viral capsid, glycoprotein, and tegument proteins were colocalized with Golgi-endosome super-mini-stacks in both the presence and absence of microtubules, suggesting that this membrane complex serves as a site of cytoplasmic envelopment regardless of clustering at the MTOC. Formation of these stable Golgi-endosome associations did not require viral capsids. Neither actin filaments nor acetylated microtubules colocalized with Golgi-endosome super-mini-stacks, suggesting that cytoskeletal elements are not required for this association.IMPORTANCEMany viruses remodel host cytoplasmic membranes to facilitate their assembly. Elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying this remodeling may reveal novel antiviral targets while also providing insight into fundamental principles of intracellular membrane organization. Infection with an important human pathogen, herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), induces extensive membrane remodeling that leads to the formation of the cytoplasmic viral assembly compartment (cVAC) in neuronal cells, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that HSV-1 induces stable associations between membranes within the cVAC. Our findings support a model in which HSV-1 generates a dynamic hybrid membrane compartment during infection, potentially reconciling conflicting views on the roles of distinct membrane sources in cytoplasmic assembly.

articles.title: Temporal dissection of hepatitis C virus and orthoflavivirus infections by continuous luminescence monitoring.
articles.abstract: Virus infection is a dynamic process consisting of rapidly evolving viral and host events, yet conventional endpoint assays provide only fragmented snapshots of these processes. Here, we established a unified temporal framework for dissecting virus-host interactions by integrating continuous bioluminescence monitoring with molecular and functional analyses. Real-time monitoring of hepatitis C virus (HCV) single-round infectious particles (SRIPs) revealed a biphasic replication profile consisting of an initial transient phase, followed by replication-dependent amplification. This transition was independently validated by similar HCV RNA kinetics observed after infection with HCV SRIPs or fully infectious HCV. Extension of this approach to dengue, Zika, and yellow fever virus SRIPs demonstrated that infection kinetics are determined by virus-specific replication programs and are modulated by the combination of viral replicons/capsids and prM/E proteins. This temporal framework enabled the identification of virus-host interactions that are difficult to resolve by conventional endpoint analyses. Early-phase cytoplasmic proteomics, combined with functional screening, identified the dynein light chain component DYNLRB2 as a previously unrecognized negative regulator of early HCV infection. Continuous monitoring also distinguished phase-specific antiviral activities, revealing distinct kinetic inhibition profiles for daclatasvir, acetylsalicylic acid, and interferon-α. Furthermore, delayed activation of the ER stress sensor ATF6 was first detected 40-47 h after HCV infection, and transcriptomic analysis at reporter-defined time points characterized the accompanying transition in host gene expression. Together, our study establishes continuous temporal monitoring as a general strategy for resolving dynamic virus-host interactions and for uncovering molecular events that remain obscured by conventional endpoint analyses.IMPORTANCEViral infection is a dynamic process in which entry, genome amplification, host-factor requirements, antiviral effects, and cellular responses occur on different timescales. Conventional endpoint assays can identify changes in these processes but provide limited information about when they emerge or transition from one stage to another. Here, we show that continuous monitoring, when combined with direct molecular and functional measurements, can place these otherwise separate observations within a common temporal framework. Using HCV and related orthoflavivirus SRIPs, we resolved early and replication-associated phases, identified host factors with stage-dependent effects, and distinguished profiles of antiviral inhibition. We further showed that ATF6-mediated ER stress activation emerged later than early HCV infection and viral RNA amplification. Thus, continuous temporal monitoring provides a general strategy for resolving dynamic virus-host interactions by defining the temporal relationships among viral processes, pharmacological effects, and host responses that remain obscured by conventional endpoint analyses.

articles.title: Superinfection exclusion strategy of siphophage T5: analysis of the FhuA:Llp complex.
articles.abstract: Superinfection exclusion is a widespread viral mechanism that protects the infected cell from overinfection by other identical or closely related viruses. Shortly after infection by bacteriophage T5, the bacterium Escherichia coli produces Llp, encoded by the newly injected viral genome. Llp is a small lipoprotein targeted to the inner leaflet of the host outer membrane. It binds to FhuA, an outer-membrane iron-ferrichrome transporter, which is the T5 receptor at the E. coli cell surface. The interaction between Llp and FhuA prevents any further bacteriophage binding and infection. Here, we determined the NMR structure of Llp and analyzed the formation of the FhuA:Llp complex using a wide range of techniques and mutants, both in vivo and in vitro. Interaction of Llp with FhuA is governed by a two-step equilibrium with a strong contribution of induced fit: Llp binding requires remodeling of FhuA periplasmic plug surface, enabling the subsequent large conformational reorganization of the extracellular loops. Analysis of FhuA mutants shows the importance of the intertwined interactions between the extracellular loops and the plug in the communication between the periplasmic and the extracellular faces of FhuA.IMPORTANCEBacteriophages (phages) are viruses that infect bacteria. As their enemies, phages play an important role in the dynamics, diversity, evolution, and pathogenicity of bacterial populations, but also represent an alternative to antibiotics in our fight against the rise of multi-resistant pathogenic bacterial strains. Infection is triggered by phage recognition of a receptor at the host surface, inducing phage DNA injection into the bacterial cytoplasm. The host cell is then transformed into a viral factory. To secure this viral factory, the infecting phage develops superinfection exclusion strategies, preventing other phages from interfering. Understanding how phages achieve the "locking" of the host will allow us to optimize phage use in phage therapy. Here, we analyze the structure of the receptor-exclusion protein complex using integrated in vivo, biochemical, and biophysical approaches. Our analysis reveals an unusually slow association process, consistent with an induced-fit mechanism, ultimately transmitting information from the bacterial periplasm to its surface.

articles.title: Gesture-based rehabilitation as an assistive technology for post-infectious and post-critical illness disabilities: opportunities and challenges.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This commentary examines gesture-based rehabilitation (GBR) as an assistive technology within an ecosystem for survivors of infectious diseases with neurological disabilities. It describes the roles of computer vision, markerless motion capture, depth cameras, artificial intelligence-driven pose estimation, wearable sensors, smartphone-based tracking, and virtual or augmented reality, while considering infection control and global accessibility.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: This commentary was developed by synthesising the existing literature, with an emphasis on camera-based motion capture, gesture-controlled serious games, AI-driven pose estimation, wearable movement sensors, smartphone tracking, and virtual or augmented reality rehabilitation systems. The analysis compares outcomes from traditional neurological conditions, such as stroke and Parkinson's disease, to the specific needs of infectious disease survivors.

RESULTS: Evidence from stroke, Parkinson's disease, and other neurological populations suggests that gesture-based systems may support motor rehabilitation, patient engagement, and remote monitoring. GBR may also reduce the need for direct patient-therapist interaction. However, there is currently insufficient direct evidence on the effectiveness, safety, and feasibility of these systems among survivors of infectious diseases. Additional barriers include hardware costs, limited digital infrastructure, and unequal access in rural and resource-constrained settings.

CONCLUSION: GBR offers a versatile method for aiding recovery after infectious neurological illnesses. Nonetheless, its safety, effectiveness, and practicality in these groups remain uncertain, as most evidence comes from non-infectious neurological conditions. Specific studies on these populations are necessary before routinely recommending these technologies, along with strategies to overcome technological, financial, and access-related challenges.

articles.title: Syncrip coordinates with hnRNPK to regulate PPV NS1 mRNA splicing and facilitate viral replication.
articles.abstract: Porcine parvovirus (PPV) relies on alternative splicing of the nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) transcript to generate nonstructural protein 2 (NS2), but the host factors coordinating this process remain incompletely defined. Here, we identified heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein K (hnRNPK) as a regulator of PPV NS1-to-NS2 mRNA splicing in PK-15 cells. hnRNPK specifically associated with NS1 mRNA, and PPV infection increased hnRNPK expression in a time- and multiplicity-of-infection-dependent manner. hnRNPK overexpression decreased the NS1/NS2 mRNA and protein ratios and increased viral DNA accumulation, whereas hnRNPK knockout produced the opposite effects. hnRNPK and the previously identified splicing regulator synaptotagmin-binding, cytoplasmic RNA-interacting protein (Syncrip) additively promoted NS1-to-NS2 splicing and PPV replication. Double-knockout and reconstitution experiments further showed that co-expression of hnRNPK and Syncrip restored NS2 production and viral replication more effectively than either factor alone. Domain-mapping analyses identified the K-protein interaction region (KI) of hnRNPK and the RNA recognition motif 2 (RRM2) region of Syncrip as the principal regions supporting this activity. hnRNPK associated directly with Syncrip, and Syncrip was required for efficient recruitment of hnRNPK to NS1 mRNA. In addition, hnRNPK associated with serine- and arginine-rich splicing factor 1 (SRSF1) in an RNA-independent manner during PPV infection. These findings support a model in which a Syncrip-hnRNPK complex promotes PPV NS1-to-NS2 alternative splicing and thereby facilitates viral replication, while identifying SRSF1 as a candidate component of the associated host splicing machinery.IMPORTANCEPorcine parvovirus (PPV) causes reproductive failure in swine and relies extensively on host RNA-processing machinery because of its limited coding capacity. Alternative splicing of the PPV nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) transcript generates nonstructural protein 2 (NS2), but the host factors controlling this process remain poorly defined. Here, we identify heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein K (hnRNPK) as a host regulator of PPV mRNA splicing and replication. hnRNPK acts additively with synaptotagmin-binding, cytoplasmic RNA-interacting protein (Syncrip) to promote NS1-to-NS2 mRNA splicing, increase NS2 production, and support viral DNA replication. Syncrip facilitates the association of hnRNPK with NS1 mRNA, and defined regions within both proteins contribute to this activity. hnRNPK also associates with the cellular splicing factor serine- and arginine-rich splicing factor 1 (SRSF1) during PPV infection. These findings reveal a host RNA-binding protein network that PPV exploits to expand its coding capacity and promote replication.

articles.title: Five ways to find a parasite: comparison of five molecular assays for the detection of Strongyloides spp.
articles.abstract:
UNLABELLED: Strongyloidiasis, caused by nematodes of the genus Strongyloides, is a neglected tropical disease with significant public health implications. Accurate diagnostics are essential for disease surveillance and control, yet traditional stool-based and serological methods have limitations in sensitivity and specificity. Molecular assays offer an alternative diagnostic approach. In this study, we compared four probe-based real-time PCR (qPCR) assays and one loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) assay using human fecal DNA samples from Gabon and Papua New Guinea with both Strongyloides stercoralis and Strongyloides fuelleborni infections. Our results revealed discordance between assays, with no single primer set identifying all positive samples across all assays. One assay was identified as specific for S. stercoralis only, while other assays amplify other Strongyloides spp. This may impact the specificity of molecular diagnostics in epidemiological surveys, particularly with increasing identifications of S. fuelleborni infections in humans from Asia and New Guinea. Of the assays examined, four were probe-based qPCR assays and a LAMP assay. On sequencing positive amplicons, enteric bacterial sequences were identified for two assays. However, subsequent testing and BLAST results identified that including a probe, as the assays were designed, would increase specificity, so that the bacterial sequences would not be amplified. These findings provide a context for the interpretation of results from various Strongyloides molecular assays.

IMPORTANCE: Strongyloidiasis is an underdiagnosed neglected parasitic infection that poses a growing challenge for public health surveillance and control, particularly in regions where multiple Strongyloides species exist and clinical case detection is challenging. Molecular assays are increasingly used as reference diagnostic tools, yet their performance and species specificity have not been systematically evaluated across diverse endemic settings. In this study, we tested the hypothesis that commonly used molecular assays differ in their ability to accurately and consistently detect and discriminate Strongyloides stercoralis and Strongyloides fuelleborni in human fecal samples. By comparing five molecular assays using samples from Gabon and Papua New Guinea, we demonstrate discordance between tests, including species-dependent detection biases. These findings provide evidence that molecular diagnostics may misrepresent species distribution. Our results highlight the necessity for awareness of target species specificity and for regionally validated molecular tools to ensure the reliable interpretation of assay results.

articles.title: Nitrate potentiates kanamycin activity in bacteria through metabolic reprogramming and CpxR-associated respiratory activation.
articles.abstract: Antibiotic resistance in foodborne bacteria profoundly compromises the effectiveness of antimicrobial therapies and represents a persistent global threat to public health and livestock production. There is therefore an urgent need to develop adjuvant strategies that can improve the activity of existing antibiotics against drug-resistant pathogens. In this study, comparative proteomic profiling of kanamycin-susceptible and laboratory-passaged kanamycin-resistant Salmonella enterica serovar Enteritidis (S. Enteritidis) revealed coordinated differences in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, nitrogen metabolism, and the respiratory electron transport chain. The resistant strain displayed reduced NADH production, proton motive force (PMF), and intracellular kanamycin accumulation. Because these proteomic analyses were performed under antibiotic-free conditions and whole-genome sequencing was not conducted, these differences are interpreted as physiological features associated with the resistant phenotype rather than as evidence of the specific genetic mechanism responsible for the increased kanamycin MIC. Mechanistically, nitrate acted as a potent kanamycin adjuvant by increasing cellular bioenergetic activity through the nitrate-glutamine-glutamate-associated pathway. Nitrate increased NADH production, enhanced TCA cycle activity, and elevated PMF, thereby increasing intracellular kanamycin accumulation. Nitrate also altered CpxR-associated regulation of respiratory genes, providing an additional route by which respiratory activity could be enhanced. Genetic disruption of nitrate transport or selected metabolic and regulatory components attenuated nitrate-mediated potentiation, supporting contributions from both metabolic flux and CpxR-associated respiratory regulation. Importantly, nitrate enhanced kanamycin-mediated killing not only in the laboratory-derived Kana-R strain but also in kanamycin-susceptible Kana-S, indicating a general kanamycin-potentiating effect rather than specific reversal of an acquired resistance mechanism. The nitrate-kanamycin combination also improved treatment outcomes against clinically resistant S. Enteritidis isolates, including increased survival in murine and chicken infection models. Collectively, these findings identify nitrate as a metabolic adjuvant that can potentiate kanamycin activity by increasing bacterial bioenergetics and drug accumulation. They further illustrate how bacterial physiological state can modulate aminoglycoside efficacy without establishing that nitrate reverses the underlying genetic mechanism of kanamycin resistance.IMPORTANCEAntibiotic efficacy is influenced not only by inherited resistance determinants but also by the physiological and metabolic state of bacterial cells. Our study shows that nitrate can potentiate kanamycin activity in Salmonella enterica serovar Enteritidis by enhancing central metabolism, respiratory activity, proton motive force, and intracellular drug accumulation. This potentiation was observed in both a kanamycin-resistant laboratory-passaged strain and a kanamycin-susceptible strain, supporting a general adjuvant effect rather than specific reversal of a defined resistance mechanism. The nitrate-kanamycin combination also improved outcomes in animal infection models using resistant strains. These findings identify inorganic nitrogen metabolism and CpxR-associated respiratory regulation as potential leverage points for developing aminoglycoside adjuvant strategies.

articles.title: Phenotypically diverse Klebsiella pneumoniae urinary tract infection isolates consistently cause pyelonephritis.
articles.abstract: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are a significant public health burden that impact millions of people every year and are highly prevalent among hospital-acquired infections. Klebsiella pneumoniae is globally the second most common cause of UTIs after uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC). Thus far, the molecular mechanisms underlying pathogenesis are better understood in UPEC than in K. pneumoniae. UPEC is known to have virulence phenotypes such as fimbrial adhesion and evasion of complement-mediated killing. In other infection types, K. pneumoniae fitness has been associated with mucoidy and diverse capsular serotypes. To establish K. pneumoniae virulence phenotypes contributing to UTI, we examined how environmental cues regulate urovirulence-associated phenotypes in clinical K. pneumoniae UTI strains. These phenotypes included capsular polysaccharide properties, hemagglutination, serum resistance, adherence to bladder epithelial cells, and in vivo fitness. We found that clinical K. pneumoniae UTI isolates' phenotypes are highly heterogeneous and can change in response to human urine. Despite K. pneumoniae clinical isolates presenting heterogeneous fitness properties, all similarly colonize the urinary tract. These results suggest that additional fitness factors contribute to K. pneumoniae uropathogenesis. Identifying these shared fitness factors will provide mechanistic insights into Klebsiella uropathogenesis and reveal candidate therapeutic targets.

articles.title: No strain, no gain: within-host bacterial microdiversity and human health.
articles.abstract: It is well established that within a bacterial species, genotypic and phenotypic variation leads to differences in virulence, antibiotic susceptibility, and metabolism. However, there is also increasing evidence that often multiple variants of the same species co-inhabit the same site in the human body, both during health and disease. This within-host microdiversity can develop over time for pathogens in chronic infections and has been observed for many members of the microbiota, for instance in the gut and on the skin. Research is just beginning to uncover how this within-host intra-species diversity develops and why it matters. Intra-species diversity is largely stable over time, with occasional selective sweeps of new genotypes, and the overall level of diversity is modulated by both microbe-microbe and microbe-host interactions. Furthermore, data indicate that within-host microdiversity can impact the stability of bacterial communities, their antimicrobial resistance, and the efficacy of probiotics and microbiota transplants. Here, we describe the evolutionary and ecological processes that promote high or low within-host microdiversity and the extent of this diversity in the human microbiota and in infections. In addition, we consider how microdiversity within individuals shapes the functional role of the human microbiota and the progression of disease. Together, within-host microdiversity is a newly developing way to think about the diversity of human-associated microbes, with implications in how we treat chronic infections and manipulate our microbiota to promote health.

articles.title: Host-secreted lactate during respiratory viral infection diminishes macrophage antibacterial activity through metabolic reprogramming.
articles.abstract: In polymicrobial infections, how the host recognizes and responds to pathogens influences which species will persist to cause chronic infections. The human respiratory tract is a common anatomical site for viral-bacterial co-infections, where primary viral infections predispose to secondary bacterial infections, leading to increased morbidity and mortality. Additionally, co-infections are disproportionately prevalent in people with chronic lung diseases, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and cystic fibrosis. We previously reported that primary viral infections and antiviral interferon (IFN) signaling stimulate Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilm formation on airway epithelial cells (AECs). IFN signaling induces aerobic glycolysis in AECs and generates lactate as a cellular byproduct. Given that innate immune systems play an integral role in co-infection dynamics, we investigated the role of host-secreted metabolites (i.e., lactate) on innate immune cell activity during respiratory co-infections. We found that exposure to the apical secretions from IFNβ-treated AECs significantly compromised macrophage antibacterial activity, with the soluble metabolite lactate playing an important role. Macrophages used monocarboxylate transporters (MCTs) and G-protein receptors to transport and/or sense lactate, respectively, and this exposure to lactate diminished their bacterial-killing activity in a time exposure-dependent manner. Lactate exposure particularly reprogrammed macrophage cellular metabolism toward a metabolically uncoupled state by increasing oxidative phosphorylation, fatty acid oxidation, and downregulating the proinflammatory antimicrobial functions. Collectively, these findings provide insights into metabolites as complex regulators of trans-kingdom interactions and epithelial-macrophage crosstalk during respiratory co-infections.

articles.title: Continuous intrathecal therapy for refractory cancer pain: A systematic review and meta-analysis focusing on partially implanted devices.
articles.abstract:
CONTEXT: Conventional pain therapies sometimes fail in patients with severe neuropathic pain or bone metastases. Intrathecal therapy provides an alternative but is resource-intensive, technically demanding and costly.

OBJECTIVE: To compare the advantages and limitations of partially implanted devices (PIDs) versus conventional medical management or totally implanted devices (TIDs) in adults with cancer-related pain.

METHODS: A systematic literature review up to September 2024 was conducted, with an updated search performed in August 2026. Eligible studies included those on adults with refractory cancer pain receiving PID intrathecal therapy compared with conventional therapy, and comparative studies evaluating PIDs versus TIDs. Pain intensity was analysed using a meta-analysis; a synthesis without meta-analysis was used for other outcomes.

RESULTS: Of the 1,102 records, 15 were included, evaluating pain intensity, systemic opioid dose, quality of life (QoL), depression/anxiety, functional capacity and complications in PID-treated patients. A meta-analysis of pain intensity at 4 weeks showed statistically significant reduction with intrathecal therapy, which also reduced opioid use and improved QoL. Complication rates were lower than in conventional therapy. Investigations of depression/anxiety and functional capacity were limited, with inconsistent findings. Certainty of evidence was moderate for pain intensity and QoL; low for opioid dose, depression/anxiety and complications; and very low for functional capacity.

CONCLUSIONS: Intrathecal therapy for refractory cancer pain with PIDs provides superior pain relief and improved QoL compared with the conventional therapy in patients with refractory cancer pain. Evidence for psychological and functional outcomes remains limited. Overall certainty of evidence is low to moderate, but findings support intrathecal therapy as a clinically meaningful option for selected patients.

articles.title: Debating targets for systolic blood pressure lowering in CKD.
articles.journal: Nephrology, dialysis, transplantation : official publication of the European Dialysis and Transplant Association - European Renal Association
articles.abstract: For several decades, there was no clinical-trial evidence to demonstrate that intensive blood pressure (BP)-lowering is a therapeutic strategy that prolongs survival and reduces the cardiorenal risk of patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). In 2015, the landscape changed after the publication of the SPRINT (Systolic Blood Pressure Intervention Trial). Compared with a standard (<140 mmHg) systolic BP (SBP), an impressive cardiovascular and survival benefit was observed with an intensive (<120 mmHg) SBP target in non-diabetic patients with hypertension and high cardiovascular risk provoking premature termination of SPRINT. In 2017, a prespecified subgroup analysis of SPRINT showed that the benefit of intensive BP-lowering was similar in patients with or without CKD. As expected, this landmark trial has substantially influenced the BP target recommendations from the guidelines released thereafter. In 2021, the KDIGO guideline made a breakthrough with the adoption of the intensive SBP target of SPRINT for the management of hypertension in CKD. However, other major medical panels, like ESC, ERA, NICE, ACC and AHA have been reluctant to follow the same approach and the optimal BP goal in CKD continues to be debated. In this article, we provide evidence defending and opposing the position that the SBP target in CKD should be <120 mmHg. We conclude with a consensus and suggestions for the successful implementation of this intensive SBP target in daily clinical practice.

articles.title: Targeting CLK1 by CRISPR tools and pharmacological inhibition modulates the innate immune response and dengue virus replication.
articles.abstract: Alternative splicing is a key regulatory mechanism known to be altered upon viral infection. These alterations can arise both from direct viral interference with the splicing machinery and from cellular responses such as activation of innate immunity. Here, we investigated splicing changes shared between dengue virus (DENV) infection and interferon (IFN) treatment in cultured cells, the latter serving as a model for virus-independent innate immune activation. Among the common events, we identified an increased production of non-coding mRNA isoforms from the CLK1 gene, which gives rise to a kinase that phosphorylates splicing factors including SR proteins and spliceosomal components. Consistent with this finding, IFN treatment led to a reduction in CLK1 protein levels. Using stable cell lines with CRISPR/dCas9-mediated modulation of CLK1 expression, we found that silencing CLK1 enhanced the induction of immune response genes, while its over-expression attenuated it. Inhibition of CLK1 kinase activity with the pharmacological inhibitor TG003 further potentiated IFN-induced gene expression and reduced DENV replication. Altogether, these results identify CLK1 as a proviral negative regulator of IFN-stimulated gene expression and suggest that its inhibition could enhance antiviral defenses and become a target for therapeutic strategies.

articles.title: Macrophage fate decisions during AKI-CKD transition insights from single-cell and spatial transcriptomics.
articles.journal: Nephrology, dialysis, transplantation : official publication of the European Dialysis and Transplant Association - European Renal Association
articles.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is an established risk factor for chronic kidney disease (CKD), but the cellular events that determine recovery or maladaptive repair remain incompletely defined. Macrophages are central regulators of this transition because their functional states change with time and tissue context. Recent single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomic studies show that renal macrophages cannot be adequately described by a simple M1/M2 scheme. Instead, inflammatory, cycling, reparative and profibrotic programs emerge in a model- and niche-dependent manner. Experimental studies identify early S100A8/A9-associated inflammatory macrophages, cycling states and repair-associated programs involving TREM2, MRC1/IGF1 and efferocytosis. Together, these changes define a transient reparative phase in which inflammation can resolve and tubular repair can proceed. Failure to sustain this phase is associated with persistent inflammation, fibro-inflammatory niches, CD38-high and scar-associated macrophages, and progression towards fibrosis. Spatial transcriptomics further shows that interactions with injured tubular cells, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, immune cells and platelets shape macrophage function. Although the timing and dominant populations differ across experimental models, several pathway-level programs recur. Human datasets support selected inflammatory and fibrotic macrophage states but show limited one-to-one conservation of cell subsets across species. Clinical translation will therefore require conserved macrophage programs, treatment windows and biomarkers that distinguish reparative from maladaptive responses.

articles.title: Possible novel manifestations of papillomaviral skin disease in 4 cats, including sebaceous gland adenoma, viral plaques confined to the digits, and a viral plaque containing novel cytopathic features and felis catus type 8 DNA sequences.
articles.abstract: Papillomaviruses (PVs) are associated with a variety of skin lesions in cats. Herein, is reported 4 cats with unusual lesions that were associated with PV infection. For each case, the lesions were examined histologically, and p16CDKN2A protein immunolabeling was performed. Total DNA was extracted from the lesions, and both consensus and specific PCR primers were used to amplify PV DNA. In addition, in situ hybridization (ISH) was used to try to detect PV DNA within 2 of the lesions. Two cats had benign proliferations of sebaceous glands that contained histological changes suggestive of PV infection. Lesions from both cats were found to contain FcaPV5 DNA, although ISH was unable to localize PV DNA within either lesion. Another cat had multiple ulcerated lesions that were confined to the digits. Histology of one of these lesions was consistent with a viral plaque. The plaque contained PV-induced cell changes and FcaPV2 sequences. The fourth cat had a viral plaque that contained FcaPV8 DNA sequences. The epithelial cells within this plaque contained large spherical eosinophilic cytoplasmic bodies that have not been previously described and could therefore be unique to this FcaPV type. The findings from these 4 cats expand the range of lesions associated with FcaPVs in cats and suggest that careful evaluation of epithelial skin lesions for the possibility of an FcaPV cause is warranted. It is important to determine whether lesions are caused by PV infection due to the increased likelihood that multiple lesions will develop in affected cats.

articles.title: Cerebral No-Reflow after Thrombectomy: International Delphi Consensus on Definition and Imaging Assessment.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The operational definition and imaging assessment of the no-reflow phenomenon, a potential contributor to poor clinical outcome despite successful thrombectomy, remains debated. We aimed to develop expert-based international consensus on the definition, assessment, and reporting standard of cerebral no-reflow post-thrombectomy.

METHODS: Three-rounds of a modified Delphi web-based survey was conducted among corresponding authors of peer-reviewed clinical studies on cerebral no-reflow between 2020 and 2025. Responses at each round were used to develop structured questionnaires for subsequent rounds. Consensus was predefined as ≥65% agreement.

RESULTS: Among 27 panelists, the response rate was 70%, 74%, and 74% over all rounds. There was broad agreement to conceptualize no-reflow as macrovascular recanalization with impaired microvascular reperfusion. Consensus was reached that macrovascular recanalization is ideally assessed as (1) digital subtraction angiography with expanded thrombolysis in cerebral infarction (eTICI) grades 2c without clear distal vessel occlusions and/or eTICI 3 only, and (2) absence of a wedge-shaped time-to-maximum (Tmax) or time-to-peak (TTP) delay on post-recanalization perfusion computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Regarding impaired microvascular reperfusion assessment, cerebral blood flow, and/or volume were preferred over time-based perfusion parameters (Tmax/TTP). The panel expressed a preference that no-reflow should ideally be assessed ≤6 hours post-recanalization. Pending formal validation, histopathological-radiological correlation in animal models would sufficiently validate the use of imaging-based definitions in humans.

INTERPRETATION: Based on currently available literature and expert opinions, this Delphi study provides a framework for systematically reporting cerebral no-reflow after endovascular treatment (EVT). The variability in opinions regarding quantitative thresholds highlights priorities for future methodological standardization and validation studies. ANN NEUROL 2026.

articles.title: Toward consensus on complementary feeding recommendations: findings from a national evidence-informed modified Delphi study in Türkiye.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Complementary feeding (CF) recommendations are generally based on international guidelines; however, several clinical issues remain controversial, resulting in variability in professional practice. This study aimed to develop evidence-informed expert consensus on complementary feeding recommendations and to explore the reasons underlying persistent disagreement.

METHODS: In this national evidence-informed modified Delphi study in Türkiye, 58 pediatricians working in Social Pediatrics participated in the first round and evaluated 53 statements using a five-point Likert scale. Statements not reaching consensus were revised based on participants' comments and reevaluated in a second round. Thirteen unresolved statements underwent a third round involving evidence presentation and structured online discussion with 23 participants; 22 subsequently completed the final re-rating. Audio-recorded discussions and written comments were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis in MAXQDA Analytics Pro 24.

RESULTS: Consensus was achieved for most recommendations regarding the timing of CF, developmental readiness, responsive feeding, and several feeding practices. Persistent disagreement remained for recommendations concerning formula-fed infants, infants with poor weight gain, preterm infants, baby-led weaning (BLW), vegan CF, bottle use, and selected allergy-related practices. Qualitative analysis generated five overarching themes: (1) individualization beyond fixed age thresholds; (2) balancing nutritional priorities with developmental safety and feasibility; (3) risk-stratified introduction of allergenic foods; (4) conditional rather than universal acceptance of BLW; and (5) ethical and clinical tensions surrounding vegan CF. Experts generally agreed on the underlying scientific principles but emphasized that recommendations should incorporate developmental readiness, clinical judgment, family circumstances, cultural context, and implementation feasibility rather than relying on rigid or universal recommendations.

CONCLUSIONS: Integration of quantitative Delphi findings with qualitative thematic analysis revealed that non-consensus primarily stemmed from the practical nuances of clinical execution and contextual adaptation, rather than a fundamental skepticism toward the underlying scientific data. These findings provide an evidence-informed foundation for developing context-sensitive CF recommendations for clinical practice.

articles.title: Host-mediated filtering and interspecific associations structure strongyle parasite communities in Sable Island horses.
articles.abstract: Mixed-species parasite infections are common in wildlife, yet the ecological processes that structure these communities remain poorly understood. We hypothesized that host-mediated and extrinsic environmental filtering, alongside biotic interactions, act concurrently to shape parasite community composition, and that these structuring patterns would depend on parasite traits or evolutionary history. We applied nemabiome DNA metabarcoding to 3147 faecal samples from 916 feral horses with no history of anthelmintic treatment, collected over 10 years as part of a long-term individual-based study on Sable Island, Canada. Using joint species distribution models, we tested whether strongyle parasite communities were structured by host-associated factors, extrinsic environmental variables or interspecific interactions. Host factors, particularly age and individual identity, explained the greatest proportion of variation in both parasite prevalence and infection intensity, indicating strong host-mediated environmental filtering. In contrast, spatial location and year explained minimal variation, suggesting weaker effects of extrinsically mediated environmental filtering. Parasite traits such as body size and gut site preference had limited associations with species' environmental responses. Positive species associations were common, particularly among species occupying the same gut region, suggesting that strong, consistent competitive interactions were not prominently reflected in the residual covariance structure. Negative associations were less frequent but consistently involved Strongylus equinus, indicating potential context-dependent biotic interactions involving this species. By integrating species-level molecular data with hierarchical joint species models, this study quantifies patterns of host-related filtering and species co-variation within a natural parasite community and provides a framework for examining mixed infections in wild systems.

articles.title: Ventricular IKur: The unwelcome guest.
The European Society for Paediatric Infectious Diseases (ESPID) - a brief reflection on its history.
articles.journal: Journal of the Pediatric Infectious Diseases Society

articles.title: A Tribute to Jon Conte: Editor of the Journal of Interpersonal Violence.
articles.abstract: Jon Conte was a pioneer in recognizing the importance of interpersonal violence and establishing the Journal of Interpersonal Violence in 1986. For this festschrift, authors were asked to identify a research question or questions that need to be addressed in understanding, preventing, and responding to interpersonal violence. I have chosen to focus on two questions that both deal with the impact of the sources of information used to understand the consequences of childhood maltreatment. The issue is that the sources of information may themselves influence study findings. In the context of existing research, two questions are addressed: (1) What explains race disparities in arrests for violence for Black and White maltreated children? and (2) How do the limitations of the accuracy of recall influence the results of studies under the umbrella of interpersonal violence and how do these limitations affect the interpretation of the results and implications drawn?

articles.title: Cardiometabolic Assessment in Patients with Overweight, Obesity, or Type 2 Diabetes Undergoing Artificial Intelligence-Based Retinal Screening: A Real-World Evidence Study.
articles.abstract: Background: Overweight, obesity, and type 2 diabetes (T2DM) increase the risk of vascular complications, including retinal vascular alterations. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based retinal screening enables early detection of microvascular damage, potentially contributing to appropriate cardiometabolic prevention strategies. We performed a realworld evidence observational study to assess cardiometabolic parameters as well as retinal vascular alterations using novel AI-based retinal imaging.Methods: Between September and December 2025, we recruited 301 consecutive adults with overweight,obesity, or T2DM; cardiometabolic assessment was performed, and all participants also underwent retinal screening with the Aireen AI system, distinguishing those who resulted positive (n = 42), negative (n = 204), or undetermined (n = 55) at the screening.Results: All patients who resulted positive at the screening were confirmed with a diagnosis of retinal alterations by the ophthalmologists. The presence of positive retinal screening (RS+) progressively increased with worsening fasting glycemia, glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels, carotid intima-media thickness, and endothelial function (P < 0.001 for all). Multivariate logistic regression analysis revealed independent associations of RS+ with HbA1c [odds ratio (OR) 2.29, P < 0.001], carotid stenosis (OR 1.06, P < 0.001), fasting glucose (OR 1.02, P < 0.001), and the triglyceride/high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio (OR 2.19, P = 0.010).Conclusions: These findings suggest that AIbased retinal screening with advanced tools can effectively identify early microvascular damage in individuals with overweight, obesity, or T2DM, with RS+ prevalence reflecting glycemic burden and vascular dysfunction. Therefore, integrating AI retinal assessment into cardiometabolic prevention programs may enable timely interventions to prevent progression to vision-threatening complications and support comprehensive cardiovascular risk management.

articles.title: Behavioral Determinants of Asymptomatic Chlamydia and Gonorrhea Among People Living With HIV in Thailand: A Cross-sectional Study.
articles.journal: The Journal of the Association of Nurses in AIDS Care : JANAC
articles.abstract: Asymptomatic sexually transmitted infections (STIs), particularly Chlamydia trachomatis (CT) and Neisseria gonorrhoeae (NG), remain common among people living with HIV (PLHIV). To determine the prevalence of asymptomatic CT/NG infections and identify associated behavioral factors among PLHIV using Pender's Health Promotion Model, our cross-sectional study included 657 asymptomatic PLHIV enrolled in an ongoing cohort at a HIV research center in Bangkok, Thailand. Participants underwent CT/NG nucleic acid amplification testing and completed behavioral questionnaires. Modified Poisson regression estimated adjusted prevalence ratios. CT-only, NG-only, and dual CT/NG infections were identified in 12.2%, 6.8%, and 3.0% of participants, respectively. Overall, 16.0% had at least one asymptomatic infection. Younger age, prior STI history, and condom slippage were associated with CT/NG infection, whereas younger age and injection drug use were associated with dual infection. Routine extragenital STI screening and behavioral risk assessment should be integrated into HIV care.

articles.title: Caregivers in a Haystack? Informatics-Driven Clinical Trial Enrollment of Dementia Caregivers at Medical Visits.
articles.journal: Journal of the American Geriatrics Society
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Caregiving status is not routinely documented during clinical care, rendering caregivers difficult to identify for research and supportive interventions. We describe two informatics-based strategies for identifying dementia caregivers at their own or their care recipient's point of care (POC).

METHODS: The CommunityRx-Dementia trial was conducted at a U.S. urban academic medical center serving a predominantly Black population. Eligible participants were caregivers of a patient with dementia recruited mainly by: (1) fee-based queries of the clinical research data warehouse (CRDW) that identified patients with dementia and their listed contacts (potential caregivers) (August 2020-November 2022) or (2) no-cost self-service query using an electronic health record (EHR)-integrated cohort discovery tool that identified patients with dementia (June 2020). For CRDW lists, probabilistic matching was used to identify contacts who were also patients at the study site. An EHR dashboard displayed medical visits of patients with dementia (identified from both strategies) and their contacts (from CRDW only) to recruit at the POC.

RESULTS: A recruitment list of 8185 patients with dementia was created: 6282 from five CRDW queries and 1883 from one self-service EHR query, 20 from self- and clinician referrals. Target enrollment (N = 344) was reached in 27 months; 321 caregivers from CRDW contacts, 19 from self-service query contacts, 4 from clinician referrals. Enrollment rates were 66% (321/488) of eligible caregivers from CRDW and 48% (19/40) from self-service query. Seventeen percent of all enrolled caregivers were recruited from their own visit (28% internal medicine, 11% ophthalmology, 9% geriatrics, 5% hematology/oncology, 47% all other eligible clinics).

CONCLUSIONS: A large dementia caregiver trial achieved recruitment goals using two replicable informatics-based strategies. The CRDW strategy involved no manual EHR abstraction and enabled direct recruitment of dementia caregivers at their own medical visits at relatively low cost.

articles.title: Nursing and Peer Support Worker Collaboration in Care for Older People Living With HIV in Australia: A Qualitative Interviews and National Roundtable Study.
articles.journal: The Journal of the Association of Nurses in AIDS Care : JANAC
articles.abstract: Older people living with HIV (PLWH) face intersecting challenges of long-term viral infection, age-related conditions, polypharmacy, and fragmented care from unfamiliar specialists, often compounded by stigma and discrimination. Nurses and peer support workers provide essential support for older PLWH navigating these challenges, yet organizational, cultural, and structural factors can impede their effective cross-sector collaboration. Using in-depth interviews and a roundtable discussion with nurses, peer support workers and older PLWH, our study highlights shared strengths and goals of HIV peer support work and nursing practice, reveals perceived barriers to collaboration, and suggests strategies to improve practice together. Thematic analysis revealed four intersecting themes: different lenses; role clarity; health care culture and power relations; and leadership, coordination and trust. Strengthening collaboration in HIV care requires addressing power dynamics and using transparent, co-constructed frameworks to clarify roles and assumptions, ultimately enhancing care teams and networks to provide optimal care for older PLWH.

articles.title: Association of HbA1c with Time in Range, Time in Tight Range, Empirically Derived Continuous Glucose Monitoring Glucose Ranges, and Mean Glucose.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate how continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) glucose thresholds, sampling duration, and statistical modeling influence associations between CGM-derived range metrics and HbA1c, and to compare empirically derived glucose ranges with time in range (TIR) and time in tight range (TITR).

RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS: Out of 8160 HbA1c-matched CGM datasets from 1584 adults, CGM data from the 14, 30, and 90 days preceding each HbA1c measurement were evaluated. Associations between HbA1c and 7790 CGM glucose ranges were assessed across varying lower and upper glucose thresholds. Linear and log-linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age and race with participant-level random intercepts were compared using root mean square error and marginal R2. Participant-level derivation (80%) and validation (20%) cohorts were used for cross-validated threshold selection and discrimination analyses for HbA1c ≤7.0%.

RESULTS: Ninety-day CGM sampling showed the strongest associations with HbA1c. Log-linear models frequently provided comparable or improved fit, particularly for glucose ranges with upper thresholds below 180 mg/dL. Stronger HbA1c associations clustered around upper glucose thresholds of 155-175 mg/dL. In validation analyses, empirically derived ranges demonstrated strong discrimination of HbA1c ≤7.0% (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] 0.909-0.915), compared with 0.903 for TIR and 0.905 for TITR, although absolute differences were small. Mean glucose demonstrated the strongest explanatory performance for continuous HbA1c (marginal R2 = 0.74) and similarly strong discrimination (AUC 0.913).

CONCLUSIONS: CGM-HbA1c relationships are influenced by glucose range, sampling duration, and statistical modeling. Our findings reinforce TIR and TITR as robust CGM metrics with strong associations with HbA1c, while also showing that selected empirically derived glucose ranges can provide modestly stronger statistical alignment. These results support the continued use of TIR and TITR while highlighting how glucose range definition may refine interpretation of CGM-based endpoints in future research.

articles.title: The Association Between Serum Vitamin D and Gait Speed in a Middle-Aged and Older Taiwanese Population: A Community-Based Cross-Sectional Study.
articles.abstract: Gait speed is a key indicator for diagnosing sarcopenia, validated by both the European Working Group on Sarcopenia in Older People in 2018 and the Asian Working Group on Sarcopenia in 2019 for assessing physical performance. While global data link vitamin D to physical performance, regional sex-stratified evidence in East Asian populations remains limited. This study aims to validate and confirm the association between gait speed and vitamin D levels in a middle-aged and older population in Taiwan. This cross-sectional investigation focused on community-dwelling residents. Participants were assigned to vitamin D sufficiency (≥30 ng/mL), insufficiency (<30 ng/mL and ≥ 20 ng/mL), and deficiency (<20 ng/mL) defined by the American Endocrine Society and International Osteoporosis Foundation criteria. Analyses included Student's t-tests, analysis of variance (ANOVA), Chi-square test and sex-stratified multiple linear regression. A total of 396 participants (164 men and 232 women) were recruited, with a mean age of 65.18 ± 8.75 years; mean serum vitamin D concentration of 28.25 ± 9.45 ng/mL; and mean gait speed of 0.91 ± 0.23 m/s. A positive association between gait speed and 25(OH)D (p = 0.047), and a negative association between gait speed and age (p < 0.001) and body mass index (BMI) (p = 0.005) were observed in men. Conversely, in women, gait speed was negatively associated with age (p < 0.001), BMI (p = 0.010), hypertension (p = 0.027), and diabetes mellitus (p = 0.009). This study demonstrated a positive association between gait speed and serum 25(OH)D levels in middle-aged and older men.

articles.title: Optilume Drug-Coated Balloon for Bladder Neck Contracture Following Pulsed Thulium:YAG Laser Enucleation of the Prostate: A Single-Institution Retrospective Case Series.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Bladder neck contracture (BNC) following anatomical endoscopic enucleation of the prostate (AEEP) occurs in approximately 3% of cases and carries high recurrence rates after standard endoscopic management. The Optilume drug-coated balloon (DCB) delivers paclitaxel at dilation but has not been reported for post-enucleation BNC. We describe the first such series following pulsed thulium laser enucleation of the prostate (p-ThuLEP).

PATIENTS AND METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed 10 consecutive patients with cystoscopically confirmed BNC after p-ThuLEP at a single high-volume center (IRB 2425566-1). All underwent laser enucleation of bladder neck scar followed by Optilume DCB dilation. Data were abstracted from the electronic health record.

RESULTS: Median age was 74 years (range 59-89). Median pre-p-ThuLEP prostate volume was 80 cc (range 36-100, n = 8). BNC presented at a median of 5.8 months after p-ThuLEP (range 2.7-12.0). A 36F balloon was used in nine patients and a 26F balloon in one, at 8 to 11 atm for 5 minutes. At a median follow-up of 5.2 months (range 0.9-15.1), no patient required reintervention (0% recurrence). Cystoscopy, performed in 5 of 10 on clinical indication, showed a patent bladder neck in all. Median post-procedure Qmax was 14.1 mL/s (n = 7), and post-void residual was 23.5 mL (n = 10). Thirty-day complications after Optilume occurred in two patients (20%), both Clavien-Dindo Grade II: gross hematuria with clot retention managed by continuous bladder irrigation and urinary tract infection.

CONCLUSIONS: Optilume DCB following laser enucleation of post-p-ThuLEP BNC appears safe and feasible with encouraging short-term patency. Median follow-up (5.2 months) is shorter than the median interval to BNC presentation (5.8 months); thus, these short-term data do not establish durability. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first report of Optilume DCB outcomes for BNC specifically following AEEP. A prospective cohort trial with longer follow-up is warranted.

articles.title: Pulmonary Rehabilitation: The Year in Review 2025.
articles.abstract: Pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) is a cornerstone of therapy for people with chronic lung disease. Over the years, there has been a tremendous amount of research in the field. Researchers have studied improved delivery methods for PR that improve patient outcomes. This article will review several important articles in the field over the last year.

articles.title: Survival and mortality in adults with cancer and pre-existing mental illness across multimorbidity types: a decade of population-based data from Alberta, Canada.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adults living with cancer and pre-existing mental illness (PMI) represent a particularly vulnerable population. This study examined whether multimorbidity protects against or increases mortality among adults with cancer and PMI.

METHODS: We used Alberta Health Services administrative data (n = 15,144), to identify adults with both PMI and cancer diagnosed between 2013-2022, including demographic, comorbidity, and cancer information. The analysis used Cox proportional hazard models (HR) to evaluate the impact among different multimorbidity categories on all-cause mortality. The multimorbidity categories were classified as cardiometabolic (e.g. cardiovascular disease), musculoskeletal (e.g. rheumatic disease), chronic airway (e.g. chronic pulmonary disease), and general multimorbidity (e.g. including liver and renal disease). Multimorbidity combinations were defined as the presence of conditions across two or more categories.

RESULTS: In a cohort of 15,144 adults with cancer, 39.1% died during follow-up. In the overall cohort, compared with those without multimorbidity, adjusted models showed that multimorbidity increased mortality for cardiometabolic conditions (HR = 1.25, 95%CI 1.13-1.37), chronic airway disease (HR = 1.88, 95%CI 1.69-2.08), general multimorbidity (HR = 1.90, 95%CI 1.59-2.27), and multimorbidity combinations (HR = 2.29, 95%CI 2.08-2.51). Musculoskeletal conditions were not significant. By PMI subtype, multimorbidity combinations were consistently associated with increased mortality across mood, anxiety, substance use, and multiple psychiatric disorders (HRs = 1.67-1.91). General multimorbidity was associated with increased mortality in anxiety, substance use, and multiple psychiatric disorders (HRs = 1.72-2.74), whereas chronic airway disease was significant only in mood disorders. Cardiometabolic and musculoskeletal conditions were not associated with mortality after adjustment.

CONCLUSIONS: Different multimorbidity categories are associated with increased mortality among adults with cancer and PMI. These findings underscore the importance of jointly considering psychiatric and physical health comorbidities in cancer care.

articles.title: Efficacy of Negative Pressure Suction-Assisted Flexible Ureteroscopy for Upper Urinary Tract Calculi and Construction of a Stone-Free Rate Prediction Model.
articles.journal: The Kaohsiung journal of medical sciences
articles.abstract: This study retrospectively analyzed 92 patients who underwent negative-pressure suction sheath-assisted flexible ureteroscopic lithotripsy (observation group) and 85 patients who underwent conventional flexible ureteroscopic lithotripsy (control group). Propensity score full matching and weighted analyses were used to balance covariates. Operative time, hospital stay, pain scores, hemoglobin changes, white blood cell counts, neutrophil counts, stone clearance rates, and complications were compared, and predictive models for stone clearance were constructed. The observation group achieved significantly higher stone-free rates at 3 days (69.6% vs. 29.7%, p < 0.001) and 1 month (75.0% vs. 34.2%, p < 0.001) postoperatively. Relative to the control group, the observation group had postoperative white blood cell counts closer to normal values (9.25 ± 3.26 vs. 10.08 ± 3.78, p < 0.05), with a smaller increase from baseline (0.82 ± 4.90 vs. 2.96 ± 5.02, p < 0.05). The neutrophil percentage was also lower (0.73 ± 0.10 vs. 0.77 ± 0.07, p < 0.05), and visual analogue scale pain score was significantly reduced (2.00 ± 0.53 vs. 2.56 ± 0.89, p < 0.001). The predictive models achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.727 (95% confidence interval: 0.616-0.839) at 3 days and 0.742 (95% confidence interval: 0.630-0.855) at 1 month postoperatively, indicating good discriminatory ability. This study shows that flexible negative-pressure suction sheath-assisted flexible ureteroscopic lithotripsy improves short- and mid-term stone clearance rates in patients with upper urinary tract stones. The models perform well and may facilitate individualized clinical decision-making.

articles.title: Psychometric properties of the timed backward walk test in people with stroke.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To examine the psychometric properties of the Timed Backward Walk test in people with stroke.

DESIGN: Cross-sectional study.

SUBJECTS: 60 people with stroke and 30 healthy adults aged 55 years and older.

METHODS: Participants performed the Timed Backward Walk test and standard clinical assessments. Discriminative validity was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curve. Reliability (one-week test-retest, inter-rater, intra-rater) was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients. Construct validity was examined through correlations with motor function, strength, balance, and gait measures.

RESULTS: People with chronic stroke took significantly longer to complete the test than healthy adults (p < 0.001), with an area under the curve of 0.968 and an optimal cut-off of 7.22 s. Test-retest, inter-rater, and intra-rater reliability were all excellent. The standard error of measurement was 1.62 s and the minimal detectable change was 4.49 s. The complete time showed strong positive correlations with functional mobility and gait speed measures (ρ = 0.840-0.897) and moderate negative correlations with balance, lower-limb motor function, and ankle dorsiflexor strength (ρ = -0.408 to -0.647). The Timed Backward Walk test demonstrated excellent reliability, discriminative validity, and construct validity in people with chronic stroke. It is a feasible and sensitive complement to forward gait assessments.

articles.title: Trends in the Asthma Burden Attributable to High Body Mass Index in Children Across 204 Countries and Territories, 1990-2021: An Analysis of the 2021 Global Burden of Disease Study.
articles.journal: The Kaohsiung journal of medical sciences
articles.abstract: High body mass index (BMI) has been identified as a significant risk factor for childhood asthma. Given the rising prevalence of childhood obesity, assessing the impact of high BMI on asthma burden trends is imperative. Utilizing Global Burden of Disease (GBD) data, we estimated age-, sex-, geography-, and sociodemographic index (SDI)-stratified asthma-related deaths and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) attributable to high BMI in children (0-14 years old) (1990-2021). Health inequality was assessed by integrating SDI with the slope index of inequality and the relative concentration index. Bayesian age-period-cohort analysis projected asthma burden trends from 2022 to 2035. From 1990 to 2021, global asthma mortality due to high BMI declined, while DALYs rose. Females had higher mortality rates, whereas males exhibited greater DALY burdens. Mortality burden correlated negatively with SDI, whereas DALYs correlated positively. Cross-national inequality analyses revealed higher mortality burdens in low-SDI countries and elevated DALY burdens in high-SDI regions. Frontier analyses indicated greater mortality reduction potential in low-and low - middle - SDI areas and higher DALY mitigation opportunities in high-SDI settings. Projections suggest a continued decline in asthma mortality but a rising DALY trend from 2022 to 2035. These findings highlight persistent sex- and SDI-related disparities and support targeted strategies to reduce the global burden of childhood asthma attributable to high BMI.

articles.title: Twenty-four-hour mean blood pressure and variability combined improve the prognostic value of ambulatory blood pressure.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To determine whether adding 24-h blood pressure (BP) variability to 24-h mean BP improves the BP predictive value for cardiovascular and all-cause fatal outcomes.

METHODS: In 1993, among individuals of the Pressioni Arteriose Monitorate E Loro Associazioni (PAMELA) population, 24-h mean BP was calculated from the mean of three hourly measurements. BP variability was quantified as the weighted standard deviation of the 24-h mean BP, the 24-h average real variability and the 24-h erratic BP variations by Fourier analysis. Variability values were used after removal of the fraction explained by their linear relationship with 24-h mean BP. Data were adjusted for baseline covariates but because of within-subject comparisons unadjusted data were also used.

RESULTS: During a 24.6 years follow-up, 250 cardiovascular and 798 all-cause deaths occurred. Adding any of the BP variability measures to 24-h mean BP significantly improved the goodness of fit of the data to the Cox prediction model used to estimate cardiovascular risk and all-cause mortality. This occurred also when BP variability was added to the net reclassification improvement (NRI) index. In subgroup analysis, a significant increase in the risk of cardiovascular and all-cause mortality was consistent in subjects with both 24-h mean and variability at least at their median value.

CONCLUSION: Addition of 24-h BP variability improves the prognostic estimate of the risk of cardiovascular and all-cause mortality associated with 24-h mean BP. This supports an upgrading of information on BP variability in ambulatory BP monitoring reports to better exploit the potential of this approach as risk estimate.

articles.title: Astrocyte SMN Restoration and Forskolin Treatment Improve SMA Synaptic Pathology.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Early phenotypic presentation of central afferent synapse dysfunction within patients with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) represents a key target for therapeutic development; however, the underlying disease mechanisms remain unresolved. By further investigating motor neuron synapse and peri-synaptic astrocyte process (PAP) defects in human SMA disease pathology, we aimed to develop a novel therapeutic approach to improve motor neuron function.
